en: Auspiciousness.
Salutations to the illustrious Śrīnivāsa, the Supreme Brahman.
The fifth chapter of the Nyāyakusumāñjali.

[Objection: "Granted that all this might be so if there were proof for the existence of God; however, we do not perceive such proof. [Reply: This is not the fault of the post that the blind man does not see it. For it is said: "From the effect, from design, from support, and so forth; from words, from cognition, and from scripture..."
From the scriptural statement and from specific numerical indications, the omniscient and immutable one is to be established. //1//

[Regarding the argument: "The earth and so forth are preceded by an agent because they are effects"—there is no sublation of this [inference] because it is foundational; there is no obstruction by weaker [reasons]; there is no contradiction between its establishment and non-establishment; and non-establishment cannot be without a basis. (2)

[ku.5.603] For instance—here, what is the intention of those who raise the objection regarding the necessity of a body? Is it that, having accepted God as the subject, they argue that He must possess a body because He is an agent; and therefore...?
Because of the exclusion of a body, there is a lack of agency;
or else, having taken the earth and so forth as the subject, [one argues] that because they are effects, they must have a corporeal agent;
or alternatively, because they are not produced by a body, they are not effects.
Or is it that [the reason] proves non-authorship from that very same [fact],
or is it merely the presentation of a contrary pervasion (*viparītavyāpti*) for the purpose of obstructing the opponent's pervasion (*paravyāpti*)?

In that regard, in the first and second cases, there are the fallacies of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), sublation (*bādha*), deviation from one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), and contradiction with the thesis (*pratijñāvirodha*).
In the third case, however, if pervasion exists, this is not undesirable; if it does not exist, there is no [logical] consequence.
In the fourth case, there is sublation and inconclusiveness. (229)
In the fifth [case], there is the fault of being an incapable qualifier;
in the sixth as well, there is sublation by a pervasion whose specific instances are not apprehended.
And it is not the case that [the pervasion] has unapprehended specific instances. (230)
When a reason is apprehended through its pervasion (*vyāpti*) as possessing a specific qualification, it constitutes a counter-balanced argument (*satpratipakṣatva*).

And there exists a specific qualification in the case of the pervasion of "being an effect" (*kāryatva*), namely the inclusion of its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). [The opponent claims: "The agent is bodiless (*aśarīrin*)."
And the absence of those two [body and intelligence] in the case of the opposite [the non-intelligent] means that it is not the agent.

Now, if there were a rule that "whatever has an intelligent cause must have a body as its cause," then there would also be a rule of contraposition: "whatever does not have a body as its cause cannot have an intelligent cause either.
However, such a rule does not exist.

If it is argued that in this way the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is also obtained, we say no—because since a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), such as the sky and so forth, is possible, the status of being a purely negative reason (*kevalavyatirekin*) would be untenable. Furthermore, in the case of a positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the qualification would be ineffective;
for in that case, it is merely the exclusion of the reason that is pervaded by the exclusion of the agent.
But it has been stated that there is no exclusion of the reason in the form of the body.
Furthermore, only a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) that is pervaded [by the probandum] is useful, and not any other, because of the risk of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
By this, it should be understood that the general conclusion— that [the probandum] is absent because it lacks the pervader of that [probans]— is unestablished (*asiddha*).
For that whose exclusion cannot be established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) in the absence of something else cannot be called its pervader.

As for the contradiction regarding specific qualities, that is refuted by the fact that if a specific quality were established, it would be perceived simultaneously [with the subject], whereas if it were not established, it would not be perceived because the property-bearer and its properties are mutually exclusive; thus, such a doubt does not even arise. It might be argued: "There certainly exists a specific sub-class of 'effect' from which the fact of having a corporeal agent is inferred.

And so, the general property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) must depend upon that very [specificity] as its pervading condition. This is not so; for the mere existence of a specific instance does not render the general property non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*).
If that were the case, then when specific qualities such as fragrance, pungency, or blackness are present, the generality of smoke would not lead to the inference of fire.
Rather, when the generality of the probans operates by relying upon the generality of the probandum, how could its particularity serve as the basis for the pervasion of a particular probandum?
But it is not the case that when a particular exists, the universal is ineffective;
for that [universal] too would entail being effective in relation to another particular.

[Objection: "Fire is observed in smoke even when specific qualities such as fragrance are absent, but an agent is not observed in an effect when specific qualities are absent. [Reply: This is not so; for a specific effect is restricted to a specific cause, but this does not alter the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the general categories of cause and effect.

Is it not observed in the world that an effect exists even when there is merely a cause— for instance, a sprout in a seed, its specific variety in grain, its specific variety in rice, and its specific variety in the *kalama* rice, and so forth in great abundance?
Or where else is it seen that a substance is composed of atomic substances, or that color and other qualities are produced from eternal color and other qualities?
Nevertheless, because it does not contradict the general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*), it is indeed established.
And this must necessarily be accepted;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is accidental (*ākasmika*).
It might be argued as follows: "The ultimate point is that this 'being an effect' (kāryatva) possesses both positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).

In this regard, one doubts whether the exclusion of 'being an effect' from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa), such as space (ākāśa) and so forth, results from the exclusion of an agent (kartṛ), or rather from the exclusion of causes in general. This is incorrect, because an agent is also a cause;
and among causes, the absence of even any single one is a necessary factor for the non-production of an effect.
Otherwise, the status of being a cause would be contradicted,
and there would arise the contingency of doubt regarding its distinction from instruments and other such factors;
for how could it be ascertained whether [the ether] is excluded from being a cause by virtue of being space?
Is it by the exclusion of being an effect (*kāryatva-vyāvṛtti*), or by the exclusion of being an instrument (*karaṇa-vyāvṛtti*)?

Likewise, is it by the exclusion of being a material cause (*upādāna-vyāvṛtti*), or by the exclusion of being a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-vyāvṛtti*), or by the exclusion of being an efficient cause (*nimitta-vyāvṛtti*)?

Because [the self] is an effect, its status as an instrument (*karaṇa*), material cause (*upādāna*), non-inherent cause (*asamavāyin*), or efficient cause (*nimitta*) with respect to cognition and so forth would not be established.

If it were established that the agent is a cause, then all this would be appropriate; but if that itself is unestablished—then is the weaver and so forth truly not a cause at all with respect to cloth and the like, but merely an agent?
Is he who has begun to establish [the point] remaining indifferent to the matter at hand?
Therefore, this too is trivial.
Now, is the agent the director of the causes, either directly, like a body, or...
Or is it through a series of effects, as in the case of a staff and so forth?
In that regard, the former [alternative] is not tenable, because it would entail the absurd consequence that atoms and the like constitute a body.
Not the second,
because of the absence of a door;
for in the absence of anything directly presided over by someone, presiding through a succession of intermediaries is not possible.
Therefore, this is the meaning of the proof: atoms and so forth are not directly presided over by a conscious being, because they are other than a body;
for whatever is directly presided over [by a conscious being] is not like this, as is the case with our own body.
Nor can they be governed through a succession [of intermediaries],
because in their own activity they do not depend on a body, just like our own bodies in their own movements; or else, the staff and so forth serve as counter-examples.
And thus,

[the argument] that earth and so forth do not have a conscious being as their superintending cause because they have causes other than a body, is countered by an equally valid opposing reason (*satpratipakṣa*) due to excessive logical pressure.
Furthermore, in the case of cloth and the like, for what purpose does the weaver and so forth require the superintendence of an agent?
Is it because those insentient things do not act by themselves,
or because they are instruments?
Not the former, for they are presided over by the Supreme Lord alone.
For it is not possible that his knowledge, desire, or effort does not pervade the shuttle and other tools;
nor do those things thus presided over require another presider for that very same purpose, because if that were the case, there would be no distinction [from the infinite regress].

Not the second [alternative], because it would entail that being a presiding agent (*adhiṣṭhātṛtva*) is not a necessary factor, which results in the example being devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
Nor should it be argued that its requirement is solely by way of being a cause; for if that were so, the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) would be: "whatever is an effect is caused."
But it is not [the case that it is] "possessing an agent"; for if one were to employ that very [reasoning], it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*).

Furthermore, the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*), which relies upon the pervasion conditioned by having an impermanent effort as its antecedent, is not intrinsically connected (*svabhāvapratibaddha*) with having an intelligent agent as its antecedent.
For even an impermanent effort does not require intelligence as its cause in the same way that a body does; such that, upon the cessation of that [effort], [the effect] would no longer be an effect.

As for the claim that "the intellect does not cease," this has already been largely refuted previously and requires no further response. For instance, if it is intended to prove a direct supervisor, it follows that atoms and so forth would have to be bodies; but what, then, is this "being a body"?
What follows [from this]?
If it is direct control by one possessing effort,
that is indeed accepted.
Nor is there anything else that would entail such a consequence.
What then of the fact that [the sense organs] are the substrata of the senses (*indriyāśrayatva*)?
That is not so, because the senses are utilized by way of generating cognitions delimited by them.
This injunction does not apply to an uninterrupted effort, because it is eternal;
for this very reason, it does not depend upon an object (arthāśrayatva).
Indeed, eternal cognition is neither of the nature of experience nor of the nature of non-experience.
It depends upon effort,
because that [effort] is a specific cause;
and there is not even the possibility of experience for one who is eternally omniscient.

In the absence of the non-perception of specific qualities, there is no occasion for false knowledge; in the absence of false knowledge, defects do not arise; and in the absence of defects, dharma and adharma do not exist.

Therefore, the two reasons—“because it is not directly presided over by effort” and “because it does not depend on that [effort] in its own operation”—are non-different from the probandum (*sādhyāviśiṣṭa*).

Furthermore, the triad of reasons—“because they are not the substrata of the sense organs,” “because they are not the locus of experience,” and “because they do not depend on those [sense organs] in their own operation”—is also established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*).

Because it is a locus of experience, even though it is not the support for the sense faculties, and because it does not assist in the karma of the experiencer, even though it is a locus of experience,
it would exist independently.
Since it is insentient, there would be no contradiction even if it were presided over by a sentient being;
thus, the argument "because it is produced by something other than that which is directly presided over by effort" is equivalent to the probandum (*sādhyasama*).

Furthermore, both arguments—"because it is produced by something other than the substratum of the sense organs" and "because it is produced by something other than the locus of experience"—are established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*).
Since it does not depend on [the knowledge of] effects and so forth, it might also be produced by something other than a body;
what contradiction is there in this? Furthermore, the subject (pakṣa) has an unestablished qualification (aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa).
It is not established by any means of valid cognition that anything anywhere has a cause not presided over by consciousness;
nor is the negation of having a cause presided over by consciousness the intended probandum, because that would result in the fallacy of the reason being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*).
[This is] because [the reason] is excluded even from the similar instances (sapakṣa), such as space and so forth.

As for what was further stated—namely, how there can be a dependence on weavers and the like regarding cloth and so forth—in that case, it is by way of being a causal agent (kāraka); what doubt could there be?
However, its status as an agent belongs only to that which possesses knowledge, desire-to-act, and effort, and not to that which exists merely in its own nature;
and this very [status] is what constitutes being a controller (adhiṣṭhātṛtva).
As for the objection, "If it is already presided over, what is the use of further presiding?"— is the weaver being dismissed, or is God being dismissed,
or is an infinite regress being introduced?
Not the first,
because it is established through positive and negative concomitance;
not the second, because...

If it were established that atoms have a supervisor who perceives the unperceived, then since knowledge and other qualities would have all things as their objects, the supervision of looms and such tools would also follow by logical necessity;
however, the establishment of God is not for the sake of supervising those [tools] alone.
Nor is it the third [alternative], because there is a lack of evidence for that.

If it is asked, "Even so, for what purpose does another preside over that which is already presided over by one?"—what is the answer? Is this a question regarding the cause (*hetu*) or a question regarding the purpose (*prayojana*)?
It cannot be the first, because the presiding of the Lord (*īśvara*) is eternal.
Because the presiding of weavers and others over their work depends upon their own causes;
nor is the second [alternative] tenable,
because it is evident that the attainment of enjoyment results from the production of the effect.
If it is argued that the effect could be produced by a single substratum alone—this may indeed be so;
nevertheless, even in the case of a combination (sambheda), there is no redundancy of either [factor].
With respect to dimension (parimāṇa), each [factor] is like number, dimension, and accumulation.
Because the capacity for cooperative action is established upon the perception of efficacy.
If it is argued that there is a difference in kind (*vaijātya*) in that case, then here too something similar will exist.
Furthermore, since the enjoyment achieved through physical exertion and the like would not be possible for a potter or others who do not act, the Lord is inferred as the agent for that purpose.
"Because sovereignty consists of that alone.
As for the argument beginning with "impermanent effort," etc.—this might be so if the intellect were to cease precisely upon the cessation of impermanent effort;
however, this is not the case. (238)

If it is argued that the intellect which serves as the cause ceases to exist because there is an absence of effort in one who is indifferent (*udāsīna*), we say no; for even the intellect of one who is indifferent is a cause with respect to the mental impression (*saṃskāra*). If it is argued that the intellect whose object is the causal agent ceases, we say no; for even one who is indifferent is a cognizer of the causal agent.
For we certainly do not observe that those who are not producing a jar or the like fail to perceive the wheel and other such tools.

If it is argued that the causal cognition of the agent ceases [to function], we say no; for even the cognition of the wheel and so forth serves as a cause toward the formation of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
If it is argued that the cognition of an agent ceases because it has become the cause of both the action and its fruit, we say no;
for even in one who does not exert effort, there persists the cognition of contact with a thorn, which is the cause of suffering and is itself caused by that [previous] action.

If it is argued that the experience which is the cause of the desire to act ceases, we say no; for even in one who does not act due to some particular reason, the desire to act and the cognition that is its cause can still arise.

If it is argued that the intellect (*buddhi*) ceases because its cause—the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), which is itself caused by an independent action—is absent, then it is not merely the intellect that ceases.

For in this way, the state of being preceded by an intelligent agent (*buddhimatpūrvakatva*)—which is characterized by being caused by a specific effort and desire to act, and is itself conditioned by having an impermanent effort as its cause—must cease upon the cessation of those [specific causes]; however, it is not the mere state of being preceded by an intelligent agent that ceases.

In that regard, because it is not a necessary factor (*aprayojaka*), this is the rebuttal concerning the thesis (*sādhyapakṣa*) that [the world] is preceded by an intelligent being (*buddhimatpūrvakatva*).
However, regarding the thesis that it possesses an agent (*sakartṛka*)— where "agent" primarily signifies effort (*prayatna*)— there is no doubt at all.
Because that very [relation] is not a limiting condition (*upādhi*) in that case.

By this, the following is refuted: namely, that just as "being an effect residing in the intellect" (*buddhigatakāryatva*) is the limiting condition for the relation with the body, so too "being an effect residing in effort" (*prayatnagatakāryatva*) is the limiting condition for the relation with the intellect.

For one who holds that, just as the intellect is related to the body, the cessation of the intellect follows from the cessation of the body; or just as effort is related to the intellect, the cessation of effort follows from the cessation of the intellect.
He might establish [this], and thus he could occasionally be censured.

We, however, inferring from the effect itself the agent who has understood the causal state and who employs all the causal factors whose capacities have been ascertained, are not to be attacked in that manner. In this regard:
Because that [cognition] is not its limiting adjunct (*anupādhi*).
Furthermore, effort does not depend on cognition solely for the sake of its own origination,
since it also depends on it for the sake of attaining its object.
Therefore, through effort, cognition [of the object] ceases, and with the cessation of that cognition, the cessation of effort is established; this has been explained at length elsewhere.
However, by the cessation of the cognition of an effect, only the effort directed toward an effect ceases, not that which is eternal.
And when effort is eternal, cognition must likewise be eternally active, not non-eternal.

For it is not possible for that [consciousness] to obtain its object by means of that [body], because prior to the body and so forth, such [obtaining] is impossible; and if the body were not produced, there would be no production at all. (243)
In brief, just as there is the property of not being produced by a body, so too there is the property of not being produced by an impermanent effort.
(KU 5.615) Since the reasoning of others is fallacious, the impurity of their logic is no fault;
rather, here, favorable reasoning—such as the non-occurrence of the effect—is an ornament. //3//
For if the activity of the agent were absent, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-arising of the effect;
since it is established that there is a causal relationship between the activities of the conscious and the unconscious,

just as there is the undesirable consequence of the non-arising of the effect when other causes are absent, so too is there the undesirable consequence of the non-arising of the effect when the agent is absent.
Because the agent, too, is not a cause [in this sense].
As for the one who says: "The determination of causal production through perception and non-perception applies only to two visible things, not to two invisible ones."
Because both perception and non-perception are capable of establishing only that much— affirmation or negation— just as in the cases of smoke and fire, or trembling and wind;
for smoke is the effect of fire, but not [necessarily] of the fire within the stomach.
For the trembling of a branch does not occur for one who is motionless even when it is caused by the wind;
rather, it occurs only for one who touches the ground.
Likewise here as well, it is appropriate to understand that causality belongs only to one who possesses a body.

The claim that "it does not belong to anything else" is incorrect; for perception and non-perception are the means for determining the production of that [cognition] when they have a visible object as their domain.
However, visibility itself is not the goal (*upeya*) in that case;
rather, it is the two universals (*sāmānya*) based on the visible that constitute the goal.

For when there is certainty regarding the origination of an effect from a specific cause (tadālīḍha), then everything of that same class— whether visible or invisible— is ascertained as possessing origination from that [cause],

just as you maintain in the case of touch, color, taste, and smell being the successive causes for one another; and as we maintain in the establishment of supersensuous inherence (samavāya) and so forth.
If it were not so,
then in the case of the very examples cited— fire and wind— which possess light and form, their production [of cognition] would be certain.
How can there be the accomplishment of two things whose forms have been discarded by non-perception?
That the accomplishment would be common to both the internal and the immobile— this might indeed be so, if [the accomplishment] were like an effect [produced] without a body and so forth.
Smoke and trembling could occur even without fire or wind, provided there were earth characterized by touch and velocity;
however, this is not the case.
Furthermore, it is impossible to assert that consciousness likewise deviates [from its causes]; therefore, enough with these attempts to resolve the ravings of the ignorant.

Even if that production is not established, once its inherent nature is established through the removal of various adventitious conditions (upādhi)— on the grounds that if an effect were to exist apart from a creator, it would thereby transcend its very nature, which leads to the absurd consequence (prasaṅga) of the non-existence of the effect—
all of this has been demonstrated more skillfully in the *Ātmatattvaviveka*, and thus is not elaborated upon here.

And when the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is thus established, there is no room for minor disturbances such as counter-objections (*pratibandi*), because if the connection is established, one is led to what is already accepted; and if it is not established, that very [lack of connection] prevents its establishment, so that such consequences do not arise.

[Objection: "But surely, if that [Lord] were always and everywhere without distinction, it would follow that the effect must arise at all times; thus there is a fault in the position of an independent Lord. Let it be disregarded in the case of one who is dependent [on other factors]. [Reply: This is like a child playing with the flame of a lamp while burning down a city—it is not so, because it would follow that the world, which is stable, would be entirely without a cause. This is granted to the Buddhist who says "yes" [to this consequence]. (247)
To the north, as stated previously:
"He who investigates the teachings of the sages and the instructions on Dharma by means of reasoning that does not contradict the Vedic scriptures—he, and no other, knows Dharma. (Ku. 5.618)

Scripture corroborates this very point, whereas it contradicts the deliberations of others: "With eyes on every side, with a face on every side, with arms on every side, and with feet on every side, the one God, generating heaven and earth, fans them together with his arms and wings. (Rig Veda 10.81.3)
Here, by the first [verse], omniscience is indicated through the mention of seeing with the eye as an illustration;
by the second, the quality of being an all-encompassing speaker.
By "mouth" is meant speech as a representative illustration;
by the third [hand], there is the state of being a coadjutor,
[and] by the arm, the state of being a coadjutor (or possessing the quality of cooperation).
By the fourth [member], pervasiveness is indicated,
because pervasion is indicated by the word.
By the fifth [reason], it is shown that *pradhāna* is the primary cause characterized by dharma and adharma,
for these two are its arms because they carry out the course of worldly existence.
By the sixth, it is shown that it is the presiding object over *pradhāna* in the form of atoms.
For they are designated as "winged" (patatra) because of their nature of moving, in the sense that "they fly.
In the expressions *sandhamati* and *sañjanayan*, there is a connection with a separated prefix (*upasarga*); thus, the meaning is "he joins together" or "he produces thoroughly."
The term "dyāvā" (heaven) is an indicator of the seven worlds above, while "bhūmi" (earth) refers to those below;
"eka" (one) signifies that He is without beginning.
Smṛti also states: "I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds" (Gītā 10.8), and so forth.
By this, the scriptures that establish Brahmā and others are to be understood.
Furthermore, because of their composition: "In independence, there would be an abandonment of insentience; the unseen does not destroy what is seen.
In the absence of a cause, there is an absence of an effect; however, a distinction possesses its own specific character. (4)
For atoms and the like proceed when impelled by consciousness, because they are insentient, like an axe or similar tools;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that an effect could not arise without a cause.
Because it is determined that non-conscious activity has the direction of a conscious agent as its effect,
this matter rests upon a specific kind of activity, rather than having that [activity] alone as its scope.
If it is argued that "action indeed depends upon a substratum of volition"— then what is this so-called "action"?

If it is intended to mean either (1) an action whose non-inherent cause is the contact of the self with that which possesses effort, or (2) an action whose sole cause is effort— that is not so, because that [volition] itself cannot serve as a qualifying condition (*upādhi*) in that context.

Now, if it is argued that reality (*tattva*) consists in having as its result the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful— that is not so, because it would fail to encompass [acts such as] consuming poison or hanging oneself.
If it is argued that it consists in having as its result the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired for the agent or for someone else—
in either case, there is no distinction, as this would be common to the actions of atoms and so forth.
Furthermore, because even a mistaken effort, though not corresponding to reality, depends upon the operation of consciousness (*cetanā*).
If it is argued that this [effort] consists in action inherent in the body, we say no; for then it would follow that even the movements of a dead body must be preceded by consciousness.

If you qualify this as "of a living being," we say no; for it would entail the undesirable consequence that even the twinkling of an eye and so forth must be admitted to have consciousness as their substrate.

If it is argued that [the body moves] "provided there is no application of another substance possessing touch," we say no—because this would entail the acceptance of such a state in the case of fire, wind, and so forth.
If it is argued that [it moves] "provided the body is not applied by another substance possessing touch," we say no—because the body is defined precisely by its movement (*ceṣṭā*).
And "movement-ness" (*ceṣṭātvam*) is a particular universal (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*).
If it is argued that this action is inferred [to be preceded by effort] because it is preceded by effort, we say no; for that [effort] is inferred by the mere fact of being an action.
If it is argued that it is inferred because it is preceded by an intelligent enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), then its [the inference's] basis simply rests upon that [intelligent agent].
Moreover, this much alone does not remove the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of mere action by a conscious principle through the mediation of a conscious substratum (*cetana-adhiṣṭhāna*).
Because a specific [reason] functions as a motivator for another specific [conclusion], it does not contradict the general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*);
otherwise, as has been stated, all general pervasions would be destroyed.
By this, the charge of being counterbalanced (*satpratipakṣatva*) by such reasons as "being bodiless" (*aśarīratva*) and so forth is also refuted.
In this regard, there is also a scriptural concordance: "When that God is awake, then this world moves;
when He sleeps, His self being at peace, then everything closes its eyes."
“This ignorant creature is not its own master over pleasure and pain;
impelled by God, it may go either to heaven or even to the pit.”
“Under my supervision, nature produces the world of the moving and the unmoving;
I heat [the world], I withhold the rain, and I send it forth. (Gītā 9.10)
(Gītā 9.19) and so forth.
Here, waking and sleeping represent the acquisition and non-acquisition of auxiliary causes;
ignorance and lack of effort are shown to be the causes for the impulsion by the Lord, which are common to atoms and other such entities as well.
Heaven and hell are characterized by the desirable and the undesirable;
this very foundation of all things will be further elucidated later with the words beginning "by me," and so forth.
I am not only the presiding agent over instigation,
but also over obstruction; for he who has power over something [is its agent].
It is capable of both impelling and sustaining that [body],
just as it has been shown by the passage beginning with "I am heating" (*tapāmi*) that it performs the impelling and sustaining of the lower limbs, the body, and the vital breaths.
[Ku. 5.623] Furthermore, by virtue of support (*dhṛti*):

the entire world, from the earth up to the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), is indeed presided over by a supporting effort, either directly or through a causal chain, because it possesses the property of not falling despite having weight, like the body of a bird in the sky and like objects conjoined with it.
By this, those scriptures that establish Indra, Agni, Yama, and the other world-protectors are also explained. Furthermore, the conventional usage of identity with all things—
such as "all this is indeed the Self"— is based on the penetration of everything by [the Self].
Just as a single magician [appears as] "a horse, a boar, a tiger, a monkey, a kinnara, a mendicant, an ascetic, a brahmin," and so forth—
if it is argued that this [appearance] is established otherwise because it arises solely from the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), [we reply: no.
Even if that [effort] were absent, because effort follows the positive and negative concomitance [with the result], it too is a cause for its own subsistence;
and because a single part of a cause cannot serve as a limiting condition (*upādhi*) with respect to another cause,
or else, if it were such a condition, it would follow that all [other causes] would cease to be causes.

If it is argued that the subsistence of the body is thus [dependent on the self] and not otherwise, we say no— because the subsistence of the vital breath and the sense organs is not pervaded [by such a dependence],
and because [this view] has already been refuted by the previous reasoning.
On this point also there is scriptural authority: "By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, heaven and earth stand held apart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.8.8).
Governance is the effort that takes the form of punishment:
"But there is another, the Supreme Person, declared to be the Supreme Self—
the imperishable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them."
Thus says the Smṛti (Gītā 15.17). Herein, "supremacy" consists in being beyond saṃsāra, omniscience, and so forth;
"transcendence" consists in being the object of worship for all.
"The three worlds" is an elliptical expression for "everything.
"Possession" (āveśa) is the conjunction of [the self] with that which possesses knowledge, desire to act, and effort.
Sustenance is maintenance;
immutability is the state of being devoid of adventitious specific qualities;
and sovereignty is the non-obstruction of one's volition.
By this, the scriptures concerning the Tortoise and others are also explained.
Furthermore, because of its reabsorption:
the world, from the cosmic egg down to the binary atomic compound (*dvyaṇuka*), must be destroyed by an agent possessing effort, because it is destructible, like a cloth being torn apart.
Regarding this, there is also scripture: "Pervading all beings with its own forms, it perpetually causes them to whirl like a wheel through birth, growth, and decay."
“O son of Kuntī, at the end of a kalpa all beings go to my own nature; again, at the beginning of a kalpa, I send them forth.”
(Gītā 9.7) and so forth.
By this, those scriptures which set forth the "fierce" aspect are also explained.
Furthermore, from the words [of the scripture]: "Because they are effects, sustenance and destruction likewise lack any underlying substrate. [Ku. 5.626]
By means of separation, there is also [the application] of a word and of an affix, as before. //5//

By the word *pada* (term/foot), what is meant here is the very usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), in the sense that "by means of this, the object that is a constituent of linguistic convention is reached or understood.
From this as well, the existence of God (*īśvara*) is established.
For instance, consider this skill in the manufacture of cloth and so forth belonging to weavers and others.
The linguistic usage of those who speak clearly,
as well as the usage of writing and its sequences by children—
all of this rests upon a self-dependent person (svatantra-puruṣa), because it is a form of usage, just like the skill in crafting a previously non-existent jar by an exceptionally skilled artisan.
It is like the words "Caitra," "Maitra," and so forth;
like the letters on a leaf;
and like the sequence of phoneme notation in the Pāṇinian system.
If it is argued that while linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) has a beginning, this [reality] may be otherwise and thus be beginningless— no, for that is unestablished;
this undertaking is precisely intended to prove its having a beginning.
Nor does this entail the consequence of undermining the beginninglessness of saṃsāra, for even so, there is no contradiction;
for it is not the case that because this conventional designation such as "Caitra" has a beginning, existence (bhava) itself lacks beginninglessness.
Or, if that [usage] were beginningless, then even the linguistic usage of terms such as "Caitra" would not have a beginning.
If it is argued that some person of limited vision (*arvāgdarśin*) might be the root source here, we say no—because such a person is incapable of this;
for at the beginning of a kalpa, even the appearance of a mirror-image is unestablished.
And creation and dissolution have been established.
But surely, an embodied being who is an agent of worldly activity has been understood [from scripture], whereas Īśvara is not such [an embodied being].

How then could this be so? It is not so; for an effect that follows the positive and negative concomitance of a body must itself possess that [body], since even Īśvara occasionally assumes a body by virtue of his effects, as he himself demonstrates through his manifestation of power (*vibhūti*).
Regarding this, there is also scriptural authority: "I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer, and the grandfather."
Likewise: "For if I were not to engage in action tirelessly at any time, O Pārtha, men would follow my path in every respect. (Gītā 3.23)
"These worlds would perish if I were not to perform action" (Gītā 3.23–24). By this, the *yajus* formulas such as "Obeisance to the potters, to the smiths," and so forth, are to be understood.

[ku.5.628] "Reliability" (*pratyaya*) as well—here, by the word *pratyaya*, the validity (*prāmāṇya*) that serves as the object of confidence is intended. And thus is the formal argument (prayoga): (249)
This tradition of scripture is preceded by excellence in its cause, because it possesses validity, like perception and other means of knowledge.
For there can be no confidence anywhere without a cognition of validity;
nor is there a cognition of validity that is itself unestablished.
And it has been explained that validity is not intrinsic;
nor is it the case that this is not a valid means of knowledge, because it is accepted by the great multitude of people.
Furthermore, one who is not omniscient lacks independent authority regarding dharma and adharma;
nor can it be confidently asserted that a non-omniscient being possesses such qualities.
This is also evident from scripture.
For instance: the Vedas were composed by an omniscient being, because they are the Vedas;
whereas that which is not composed by an omniscient being, [is not a Veda].
This [Veda] is not like other sentences.
But what indeed is this so-called "Veda-ness"?
For there is a contradiction between being a sentence and being a sentence whose subject matter is supersensible (*adṛṣṭa*).

If it is argued that [the definition] is incorrect because the property of being a statement that is a means of valid cognition regarding an unperceived object is unestablished—and because there is a contradiction since [the definition] would apply to the statements of Manu and others—[we reply]: No, for the defining characteristic is being a statement accepted by great persons (mahājana) while having no other perceivable source.
For the direct perception and other means of knowledge belonging to Manu and others cannot be the source [of their own statements].
Nor can it be due to delusion or deceit,
as it has been stated that [the Veda] is accepted by great men;
nor is mere tradition itself the root [of its authority].
It has been stated that [the Veda is not eternal] because it is interrupted during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*),
or by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*):
"The sentences of the Veda are of human origin, because they are sentences, like the sentences of people such as ourselves."
If it is argued that this is not so because the author is not remembered, we say no, because that reason is unproven (*asiddhi*).
For [the scriptures state]: "Immediately thereafter, the Vedas issued forth from his mouths," and "In every Manvantara, a different revelation (*śruti*) is ordained."

This is because of the Smṛti passage: “I am indeed the author of the Vedānta and the knower of the Veda,” and because of the recitation of Śruti passages such as: “From that sacrifice in which everything was offered, the Ṛks and Sāmans were born.
If it is argued that this is merely an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda), we say no; for a Smṛti that records an agent is not intended to be non-injunctive in all cases.
And likewise, because there is no recollection of [works] such as those by Kālidāsa,
it would follow that works like the *Kumārasambhava* are without an author;
or else, the logical reason (hetu) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

If it is argued that [the inference] lacks a counter-positive (satpratipakṣatva) because its object is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition (pramāṇāntara), we say no—because it is unestablished (asiddhi) with respect to the author [of the scripture], and because it is inconclusive (anaikāntika) with respect to others.
This is due to the cause of the recollection of pleasure from a spontaneous smile. (252)
For even a specific property that is not within the range of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) can be communicated by that very speaker. However,
in the present case, a speaker is simply not possible,
because in the absence of a cause, there is an absence of the result.
Because the eyes and other [senses] lack the capacity for that [perception], just like the senses of people such as ourselves;

and because the mind lacks independence regarding external objects—this is not so, for if one takes either the conscious cognition, the sense organ, or the mind as the subject of the argument, there is the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), as has already been explained in detail;
furthermore, they lack the capacity [to perceive it] once permanence has been refuted.

If it is argued that atoms and the like are not perceptible to anyone because they lack the requisite causal complex (*sāmagrī*), we say no: for this reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to the perceiver himself, while for others it constitutes proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
Even so, the status of being a sentence (*vākyatva*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
This is because it is not a necessary factor;
in that case, the quality of being human-authored (pauruṣeyatva) is caused by the fact that the subject matter falls within the scope of other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
and not caused by the fact of being a sentence— this is not so, because it would follow as a consequence that the scriptures of the Sugata and others are not human-authored.

If it is argued that [the reason] applies to that which is a valid statement (*pramāṇavākya*), we say no—because the property of having an object that falls within the scope of another means of valid cognition belonging to the author would entail the very point to be proven (*sādhyānupraveśa*).

For being composed by an independent person is indeed what constitutes "human origin" (*pauruṣeyatva*); and independence consists in the desire to speak and the exertion of effort having as their sole object the cognition of the meaning.
Furthermore, it would follow that the statements of Manu and others are non-human (apauruṣeya), because their meaning is not within the scope of any means of knowledge other than verbal testimony.

If it is argued that [the definition] merely requires that the meaning be something other than what is within the scope of the sentence currently being employed, we say no; for that condition exists in the case of the Veda as well.
Because even a single meaning is established through many statements due to the division of Vedic branches;
if it is argued, "Let it be so, but there is no relationship of root and branch between them," we say no, because this has already been answered.
Furthermore, it is also due to the specific number [of statements].
First, the dyad and the triad possess dimension because they are substances, like atoms. Furthermore, that dimension is an effect because it is a quality of an effect.
And neither the dimension of the atom nor the dimension of the dyad can be its cause.
Because it would possess eternal dimension, and because it would possess atomic dimension;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the production of an effect without a substrate.
Furthermore, it would follow that the dyad (dvyaṇuka) must possess magnitude,

because there is no distinction between it and the triad (tryaṇuka) in terms of being composed of atoms; for while magnitude in the latter case is established by the multiplicity of its causes, it has been established that atomic dimension (aṇu-parimāṇa) does not initiate [magnitude].

Nor is it tenable to claim that the very minuteness [of atoms] constitutes the distinction for the commencement of something large; for this would entail the consequence that the large could not originate from the large,
and because of the contradiction between minuteness and largeness, it would entail the consequence that they cannot produce an effect of a single homogeneous nature.
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that a composite could be produced by many atoms or even by two dyads (*dvyaṇuka*s).

If it is asked what the fault in this case would be: the consequence is that the effect of the atoms would possess magnitude (*mahattva*), because multiplicity of causes is the cause of that [magnitude].
Otherwise, if atoms were to initiate [a composite] without restriction—as by two, three, or four—then that [postulation of atoms] would result in futility.
Furthermore, the admission of a gradation [in size] belonging to the atom itself could not occur if one disregards number.

If it is argued that let there be an initiation of the "large" (mahat) by three [atoms] alone, this is not so; for there is a rule that a large effect must be initiated by an effect-substance (kāryadravya).
Nevertheless, in the case of degrees of intensity, number alone is the determining factor;
nor is accumulation to be expected, because there is an absence of conjunction between parts.
Therefore, it is established that dimension and accumulation are the originators of "large" alone.
Consequently, "multiple number" remains as the only possibility;
it is produced by relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), because it is a multiple number.
Furthermore, the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) of people like us cannot occur with respect to atoms.
Therefore, he in whom that [cognition] exists is omniscient.

Otherwise, due to the absence of relative cognition, number would not arise; in the absence of number, the dimension residing therein would not be produced; and since a substance lacking dimension cannot be a producer, the triad (*tryaṇuka*) would not be produced, which would entail the non-production of the entire universe.

If it is argued that the inferential *apekṣābuddhi* (relational cognition) may belong only to persons such as ourselves, we say no—because this would lead to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
For once a gross effect has been produced, one can infer the atoms and so forth by means of it;
yet, only when those [atoms] exist can the gross object arise through the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so on.

If it is argued that size (parimāṇa) arises from the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) alone and that there is no need for a relative cognition (apekṣābuddhi), we say no; for then one might as well claim that everything arises from that [unseen force] alone, leading to the untenable consequence that there would be no need for any perceived causes.
Alternatively, the passage beginning with "kārya" is explained in another way:
"The explanation of the Omniscient One has as its primary intent the mere enumeration [of categories];
thus, terms such as 'Īśvara' possess their conventional meaning in accordance with worldly usage. (6)
For in the case of the Veda (*āmnāya*), which has a future result as its object, human activity and cessation from activity occur with respect to what is to be done (*kārya*).

However, although that which has an already existent fact as its object does not directly possess the power to impel or restrain, nevertheless, its authority resides precisely therein by virtue of its intended meaning (*tātparya*).
For instance, it is the power of the injunction itself that, when faltering, is supported by praise and the like;
for it is a settled principle that everyone engages in what is praised and desists from what is censured.
In this context, the denotative power (*abhidhā*) of a word is its primary function; the meaning of the word (*padārtha*) is that which is arrived at through the force of that power.
Furthermore, when there is expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, the capacity for syntactic connection (*anvayaśakti*)—whether residing in the words or in the word-meanings—is the sentence (*vākya*).
The meaning of the sentence follows from that [literal] power;
however, the intended meaning (tātparyārtha) is now being considered—
that which has as its ultimate goal the thing to be established, the thing to be communicated, the purpose, or the objective.
This very thing is that supreme;
its state is reality (tattva).
That which has this as its object—
It might be argued that this is the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*).
In that regard, the first [alternative] is not tenable, because an object— that is, an action— is not something to be established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And since there is no result other than the comprehension of that [meaning],

if it is argued that the "ultimate" (para) object to be accomplished is defined as the form of engagement or withdrawal by way of communicating a praiseworthy or censurable self-interest— this is not so; for in the case of the expression "a hamlet on the Ganges," the bank, which is neither of the nature of engagement nor withdrawal and thus not itself the object to be accomplished, is nonetheless considered the ultimate meaning.

If it is argued that since activity and cessation with respect to the bank (*tīra*) are the objects to be accomplished, the bank itself must also possess "otherness" (*paratva*), we say no; for the purpose is fulfilled merely by the denotation of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Nor is the second alternative tenable, because neither a word nor a sentence has any other referent to convey apart from the word-meanings and their mutual relations.

The claim that "the other [meaning] is conveyed through the non-separation from its own primary meaning, even without the power of the word-base (pada-śakti) or the power of syntactic relation (saṃsarga-śakti)" is also not tenable; for there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) to whatever is non-separate from the primary meaning of a word. For in that case, even such expressions as "there is water in the Gaṅgā" would have to refer to the riverbank.
Because the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) remains in that same state.
If it is argued that it would be so [only] when there is a primary sublation (*bādhaka*), we say no; for it exists even when that [sublation] is absent.
For example: "Go, O beloved, if you must go; may your paths be auspicious."
"May my birth also be in that very place where you have gone"— even though the primary meaning here is not contradicted, the intention (tātparya) lies in the prohibition.
Furthermore, intention is not found only in the case of a pervasive [meaning], for it is observed even in the case of what is non-pervasive.
For example, in the expression "the beds are crying," the intended referent is the persons; yet there is no necessary concomitance (avinābhāva) between the bed and the person,
nor between the person and the act of crying.
Nor is the third [alternative] tenable;
for that [requirement] would have to be either required by the person to be informed or required by the person who informs.
Not the first [alternative]; for the validity of verbal testimony does not depend upon that [the object], or else there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For whatever depends upon something else, [that thing must exist prior to it].
Because that [other] would follow as being distinct from it.

If it is argued that there is a restriction of dependence because it is to be accomplished for the sake of that [purpose], we say no—because when the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is manifold due to the distinction between what is to be produced (*kārya*) and what is to be made known (*jñāpya*), there follows a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) owing to its having different intended meanings (*tātparya*).
For smoke, indeed, has many effects, such as the darkening of a location, the driving away of mosquitoes, and so forth.
There are many things to be made known, such as the burning of moist fuel and so forth.
Thus, when it is stated in this context that "there is the rising of smoke," what would be the intended meaning of the sentence?
For it is impossible to restrict [the meaning] by depending on the intention [of the speaker].
Nor can it be that the proponent has neglected it,
because such a thing does not exist in the Veda;
however, the fourth alternative would be possible.

Whatever word is employed with reference to a particular object, that word is intended to convey that very object; for such is the worldly understanding of linguistic usage. To illustrate: in common parlance, a statement of praise is employed with reference to the thing being described.
That which has acquisition as its ultimate purpose is so called;
a statement of censure is employed with the aim of relinquishment, and thus it has relinquishment as its ultimate purpose.
In this same manner, other cases should also be inferred by oneself.
Therefore, one must accept this even in the Veda in accordance with worldly convention;
otherwise, there would follow the consequence that the *arthavādas* (explanatory passages) would be entirely purposeless.

Since "intention" (*uddeśa*), "resolution" (*vyavasāya*), "qualification" (*adhikāra*), "aim" (*abhiprāya*), "state of being" (*bhāva*), and "disposition" (*āśaya*) are synonymous, the existence of a preeminent person (*puruṣadhaureya*) who serves as the substratum for these qualities is established.

And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Vedic statements of praise are preceded by the intention to induce acceptance, because they are statements of praise, like worldly statements such as "the mango fruit is sweet upon ripening.
Likewise, statements of censure are preceded by the intention to induce avoidance, because they are statements of censure, like statements such as "the jackfruit is bitter upon ripening.
Furthermore, the undesirable consequence of being meaningless is stated as the subverting reason (*bādhaka*) in the case of the counter-example.
Furthermore, if it were not so,
even presumptive testimony based on what has been heard (*śrutārthāpatti*) would be lost;
for an established object is indeed the domain of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
But it must not be performed by that very same [person].

Furthermore, in the case of the statement "Devadatta is fat and does not eat during the day," there is no such elliptical completion as "he eats at night," because that would be contradicted by non-perception (*anupalambha*).
Because there is an absence of the activity of the palate and other organs— the causal complex for either production or manifestation—
and because it is impossible even to suspect that which is incapable [of such action],
therefore only that which resides in the intention remains.
Because there is no other alternative;
if that [object] does not exist in the Veda, then there is no presumption based on what is heard (śrutārthāpatti), which would result in the undesirable consequence of the futility of its exposition.
Therefore, from the fact that there is an effect, and also from the intention [behind it], it is inferred that there exists an author; for indeed,
there would otherwise be no purpose.
For no one can comprehend any meaning from the Veda unless it has been explained;

nor should the explanation of one who perceives only a single portion be respected, because of the lack of confidence resulting from the maxim: "A word whose prior and subsequent context is not considered produces a different understanding."
Even from a sentence consisting of only three or four words, one who hears only a portion of it might arrive at a contrary understanding;
how much more so in the case of that which transcends the senses and is difficult to comprehend due to the intermingling of intermediate sentences?
Therefore, one must necessarily accept some person who perceives the entirety of the Veda and the meaning of the Vedas.
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of a blind tradition.

Furthermore, one who has heard, studied, mastered, and remembered the meaning of the Vedas along with their limbs (*aṅga*) and sub-limbs (*upāṅga*), or even one contrary to that, cannot possibly exist other than as an omniscient being. For who else, having not directly perceived the universe and its performance [of rituals], could [possess such knowledge]?
One should conclude that "this tradition is only this much.
Furthermore, what person of limited vision could possibly study or teach all the Vedas, either in their entirety as texts or in their entirety regarding their meaning?

Here too, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The Vedas were at some time explained by one who knew the meaning of all the Vedas, because even when there is fluctuation in the minds of those performing the rituals, the performance of the rituals remains unshakable.
Whatever is such, all that was explained by one who knew its meaning.

As in the case of the *saṃhitās* of Manu and others. Otherwise, due to a lack of confidence and a resulting absence of settled authority, there would either be a failure to practice or a state of instability, because there would be no authoritative instruction.
If it is argued that the practitioners themselves are the instructors, we say no; for their understanding is not fixed.

If it is argued that the performance of the meaning of the Vedas is also beginningless like the Vedas themselves, we say no; for that [performance] must either be independent or dependent upon the understanding of the Vedic meaning.
In the first case, there would be the consequence of its being rootless (nirmūlatva); in the second case, however, there would be the contingency of lacking any fixed rule (aniyama).

For there is no restrictive rule to the effect that, while the cognition of that [object] by the ancients is authoritative despite the lack of distinction from those who are not omniscient, it is not so for those of the present day;
this holds true even in the case of words.
For it is heard that such terms as *praṇaveśvara*, *īśāna*, and so forth exist,

and they are meaningful because they are employed without contradiction in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Itihāsas, just like words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*); thus their existence is established through direct perception.
When an inquirer wonders, "What is the meaning of this?", there arises a definitive determination,
as in the case of words such as "heaven" (*svarga*):
"But the Supreme Person is another, declared to be the Supreme Self."

This is because of the explanatory passage (arthavāda): "The imperishable Lord, having entered the three worlds, sustains them," or because of the remainder of the sentence (vākyaśeṣa), as in the cases of the *yava* and the boar.
For example, after beginning with devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*), it is heard: "Omniscience, contentment, beginningless awakening, absolute independence, and eternally unfailing power."
"Those who know the ritual rules say that the six limbs of the omnipresent Maheśvara are his infinite powers.
If it is argued that such a matter is contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), we say no—because it has already been refuted.
If it is further argued that there is no valid means of knowledge for that [matter], then what confidence can there be in the existence of heaven?
For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for people like us regarding pleasure characterized as described [in the Vedic texts].

If it is argued that it is determined to be so because the activity of the performers of sacrifices would otherwise be inexplicable, we say no—because this would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
For activity toward heaven would occur only once its nature is determined, and its determination would occur only through the inexplicability of activity otherwise.

If it is argued that there is no fault in determining [the nature of pleasure] based on the practice of those who were previously old, we say no, because this would lead to the fallacy of a "blind tradition" (andhaparamparā).
If it is argued that there is no contradiction because such a pleasure might occasionally arise for someone due to the power of specific unseen merit (adṛṣṭa),
since there is a lack of evidence to deny it— then the same applies to the other case as well.

Here too, the formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: whatever word is employed by the learned in a certain sense, even in the absence of another [conventional] application, that word is the designator of that thing;

for example, the word "heaven" (*svarga*), when employed in the sense of a particular kind of pleasure, is the designator of that pleasure. And this word [“Ishvara”] is employed in reference to the creator of the world.
Otherwise, since it would follow that [the word] is meaningless, the co-occurrence with a collection of meaningful words would be untenable.
By this, those words denoting specific deities such as Rudra, Upendra, and Mahendra are also explained.

Furthermore, our term "pada" is employed in the Veda just as it is in common worldly usage; and in the world, that term does not have any meaning other than [the sense of] a conscious entity, because it is never used in that way for insentient things.
Nor is the meaning merely the self [of the speaker], for that would entail the application [of the term] even to another's self;
rather, it is he who utters it with independence.
He states that very point: for it is determined by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) in exactly that way.
Therefore, without overstepping worldly linguistic convention, even in the Veda, the speaker must be understood as the one who employs [the words] themselves;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of improper usage.
Nor is it logical that whenever someone utters the Vedic word "I," he alone is its referent at that time;
for if that were so, in such passages as "One should worship me" (mām upāsīta), that very person would be the object of worship.
If [the meaning were] "I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds," then the succession of teacher and disciple alone would attain sovereignty over the Self,
and thus the practice of worship would become a mere madman's frolic.
Furthermore, worldly convention would be subverted.

Therefore, it is established that one who recites this [Veda] is not its speaker, but rather its author; thus, when applied in the Veda, the word "we" (asmad) denotes its own user, because it is the word "we," just as in common worldly usage.
In this way, other words as well— such as "whoever" (*yaḥ kaḥ saḥ*) and so forth— are to be understood,
because their scope is delimited by being conditioned by mental engagement, inquiry, reflection, and the like,
and because those [mental states] are properties of the speaker.

For that [action] is not merely vibration;
because it would fail to apply to such cases as "one should perceive the self," and because it would over-apply to such cases as "he goes to the village."
Nor is effort (*prayatna*) the cause of that [action], because it is common to all verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*). [Objection:
But surely, effort is not the meaning of the suffix in every instance;

In expressions such as "he does" (*karoti*), there is no [effort] that exceeds the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), because the suffix has fulfilled its purpose by denoting number alone. Therefore, [the opponent claims] that effort is expressed solely by the gender and other [grammatical] features— [but this is] not so, because the same [objection] applies even in the case of "one should do" (*kuryāt*).

If it is argued that even though mere effort (*prayatnamātra*) is the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), because it has become subordinate (*parāṅgatāpanna*) [to the action], it is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), and thus there is no equality [between the two meanings], we say: no, for even so there is equality.
Furthermore, the fact that one [element] expresses that [meaning] does not entail that the other would be its opposite.
Because there is deviation [from the rule] in cases such as *eko dvau bahava eṣiṣati* ("one desires two or many"),
if one were to postulate a desire for the number "two" and so forth in that instance, then the same would apply to cases such as *karoti* ("he does") and *prayatate* ("he exerts effort").
This is because, once the capacity of each individual element has been determined elsewhere, the postulation of such [collective] properties is identical when they are combined.
If it is asked, "What is the recourse when that [causal relation] is impossible in cases such as 'the chariot goes'?"—the answer is: it is the same as in the case of "the threads produce the cloth.

If it is argued that this is merely common worldly usage and is not to be questioned, then it is equal [in both cases]. When the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is understood through the linguistic training of elders in worldly usage to signify "that which is to be done" (*kāryatva*), everything becomes consistent.
If it is argued that this is not the case for a word merely uttered, we say no; for proficiency [in meaning] arises even from explanations and the like, and such [explanations] exist here:
"What does he do? "He cooks."

Since we see such expressions as "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*), one might argue that even so, when the verbal root denotes merely its own meaning as having attained a state conducive to the result (*phalānukūlatāpanna*), there would be the fault of conceptual complexity (*kalpanāgaurava*) in postulating the denotation of an effort (*prayatna*) distinct from that;
therefore, the paraphrase (*vivaraṇa*) also refers only to that much. If this is the objection:
This might indeed be the case if he were to explain it by means of "cooking" (pākena);
however, this is not so.
Since the meaning of the verbal root itself, as in "pāka" (cooking), is indicated as that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*),
it is logical that the suffix must denote something that has acquired a degree of favorability toward that very accomplishment.
Nevertheless, that [favorability] must necessarily be an effort (*prayatna*).
If it is asked why it cannot be [explained] by another, it is because it is explained in that specific way as a rule;
for, in the absence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), it is impossible to alter it otherwise,
as otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
This might be the case: for anyone [who holds this view], the meaning of the verbal root consists merely in bringing about a state of conformity toward a result, and not in effort itself.
For that [effort] too must be expressed by a suffix through this very same limiting condition (*upādhi*).
But it is not by the mere fact of being an effort; for that would lead to the undesirable consequence of there being no distinction from the word "effort" (prayatna) itself.
Therefore, it is better to let it be just that much for the sake of parsimony.
Otherwise, two adventitious conditions (*upādhi*)—namely, being favorable and being effort—would have to be postulated.

If it is argued that, in the absence of a subverting factor, verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) must everywhere be understood in a figurative sense when applied to insentient things, it is said in reply: [Kārikā 5.652] "By means of the distinction between what has been done and what has not been done, and by the determination of the nature of the agent..."
Effort itself is the prior volition; in relation to the subsequent [action], that very same thing is "bringing-into-being" (bhavanā). //9//

For [the term] "made" (kṛta) is used in relation to jars and the like because one recalls that they were preceded by effort; whereas even when one recalls the existence of a cause, those who lack the recollection of being preceded by effort do not apply that term to sprouts and the like. Thus, it is determined that the meaning of "to make" (karoti) is indeed effort.
Otherwise, since there would be no distinction in the fact that everything is preceded by some favorable condition, one would have to say, "Jars and the like are made... [but this is not the case].
"How could there be a rule of linguistic usage [stating] that sprouts and so forth have not been produced?

Since every verbal form (*ākhyātapada*) is explained by that [meaning], it is determined that this same meaning applies everywhere. Thus, a word that functions with respect to a whole is also employed for a single part thereof.

This is by prioritizing mere purity, just as the term *śrotriya* is applied to a Brāhmaṇa. Otherwise, even though cognitions belong to middle and superior persons, [terms like] "he knows," "he desires," "he exerts effort," "he resolves," "he sleeps," "he doubts," and so forth, when applied to non-conscious entities in the first person, have only a figurative meaning.

Furthermore, since the application [of a word] is possible even through another function (vṛtti), it is not reasonable to postulate a primary denotative power (śakti); for it is an established principle that "it is improper for a word to have multiple meanings.
For this very reason, there is also direct experience [to support this].
What is meant by "he cooks" (pacati) is that he possesses a present effort conducive to the act of cooking; likewise,
what is meant by "he cooked" (apākṣīt) is that he possessed such an effort in the past.
Thus, one who possesses such effort— past, present, or future—
is said to "will cook" (*pakṣyati*), but not "is cooking" (*pacati*) in the sense of possessing some effort conducive to cooking.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition "he is cooking" even in the case of a guest who is sleeping after another's labor.
Furthermore, the meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do) is precisely the activity of an agent (*kartṛ-vyāpāra*),
and the agent is conscious;
otherwise, the determination of that [agency] would be untenable.
For agency does not consist in possessing an activity that is being denoted by a verbal suffix,
because it would follow that one who is acting would not be an agent during a state when [the activity] is not being denoted.
Nor does agency consist in possessing an activity suitable for being denoted by a verbal suffix.

Because fitness itself cannot be established; for that which is merely "conducive to the result" is common to the operations of all causal factors (*kāraka*s). Nor is there a restriction based on the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).

Because in a state where [the agent] does not intend to speak, there would be the consequence of a lack of restriction. If it is argued that this is not undesirable in the case of its own operation— then,

by the principle that "agency exists in every factor (kāraka) with respect to its own operation," it follows that there would be the consequence of the disappearance of the instrument (karaṇa) and the other factors.
The designation of "instrument" (*karaṇa*) and so forth is not made with respect to their own intermediate operations,
but rather with respect to the principal action.
For there is indeed, for the factors of action (*kārakas*) proceeding toward a certain [principal] action, a connection with intermediate operations.

If it is argued that their activity is directed solely toward an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*), then one must consider what the cause is for the specific restriction of the conventional designations of agent, object, and so forth, based on that very [operation].
If you say it is due to "independence" (*svātantrya*), then tell me: what else is this independence other than the inherence (*samavāya*) of effort (*prayatna*) and the like?
Therefore, in all cases, the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is simply a uniform operation.
[Objection: Even so, let it be that the very conformity to the result (*phalānuguṇatā*) is the cause for the operation of the suffix (*pratyaya*);
as for effort (*prayatna*), it will be obtained by implication (*ākṣepataḥ*). [Reply: No—for in all cases, the domain of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is *bhāvanā* itself, whose essence is effort.
