For by what could that [action] be projected?
Not, first of all, by mere favorability; for that [favorability] is not coextensive with the nature of effort (*prayatna*).
For favorability (*anukūlatva*) does not consist solely in inherence in the same object as effort (*yatnatva*);
for this very reason, it is not [denoted] by number (*saṅkhyā*),
since that [number] terminates merely in what is to be numbered (*saṅkhyeya*).

If it is argued that [the agent] is [denoted], we say no; for a mere substance is not an agent. Furthermore, if that which possesses activity is denoted, one must necessarily admit the denotation of the activity itself.
Nor can that [agent] be implied by the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha).
Because that [expectation] is impossible in cases such as "it exists" (*vidyate*);
for here the meaning of the verbal root does not depend on *bhāvanā*,
since existence is eternal.

If it is argued that [the meaning] will not exist there, we say no; for there is no distinction in the experience of the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) as it occurs in a temporal sequence of before and after.
Indeed, by the coloring of cultivation, even an object that is not actually such appears as being so.
Furthermore, there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the referent of the suffix with the favorability derived from the cultivation obtained from another word.
Because that is impossible;
for it is certainly not denoted by its very nature,
since verbal roots denote only the result of an action.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even in cases such as "cooking" (*pāka*), there would be an experience of *bhāvanā*.
Nor can it be expressed by another word such as "Caitra," because both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) have as their meaning only the non-agent (*akāraka*).

Since words such as "rice" (*odana*) are *kāraka* (participant) words, and since a *kāraka* is necessarily associated with an action, its expression occurs either through direct denotation (*abhidhāna*) or by implication (*ākṣepa*). If this were not so, one might ask: why, when "rice" is mentioned, does a specific expectation (*viśeṣākāṅkṣā*) arise as to whether one "eats" or "cooks"? We say: no, for we observe that when "he cooks" (*pacati*) is said, there arises a specific expectation as to whether it is "rice" or "broth.
And this [expectation] would not occur without either direct denotation or implication.
If there is no implication (ākṣepa) in that state, then it must surely be a direct denotation (abhidhāna) itself.
It might be argued: "In that case, let the agent (kartṛ) also be directly denoted."
For if that [number] were not expressed, the number, having merely implied the object of enumeration (*saṅkhyeya*), how could it follow the agent, and not also the object (*karman*) and so forth?

If it is argued that in cases such as "Caitra cooks vegetables and soup" (*śākasūpau pacati*) or "Caitra cooks vegetables, soup, and rice" (*śākasūpaudanān pacati*), the number—being excluded from the objects by contradiction—follows the agent Caitra without contradiction; then [what happens] in the case of "Caitra cooks rice" (*caitra odanaṃ pacati*)...?

[Objection: "The meaning of a treatise determined in one place applies likewise elsewhere, just as in the cases of the words *yava* (barley/awn) and *varāha* (boar/jackal). [Response: If this were so, then the same would follow for words such as *pacyate* ("it is cooked") and so forth.
If you argue that while [the dual forms] *caitrābhyām* and [the plural form] *caitraiḥ* are excluded by contradiction, the word *sūpaḥ* (soup) follows the action without contradiction;
then what is the solution for the case of *caitramaitrābhyāṃ pākasūpau pacyete* ("by Caitra and Maitra, both the cooking and the soup are being cooked")?

If you say that linguistic usage proceeds according to a meaning determined elsewhere, we reply: no, because that would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the same applies even in cases such as *pacati* ("he cooks").

If it is argued that in this case the former [rule] alone provides the determination, whereas in the case of *pacyate* the latter does, we say no— because there is no distinction [between them]. If it is argued that the distinction lies in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) and the active voice (*parasmaipada*), we say no— because this would lead to confusion in cases such as *pacyate*, *pacate*, and *pakṣyate*.
Furthermore, the connection of number with that which is expressed by a common suffix is observed;
for example, in such cases as *bhūyate* (it is being) and *supyate* (it is being slept). For in those instances, there is no connection with an agent, an object, or any other factor whatsoever.
But it is by means of the state [of being] alone;

for if there were no connection [with that state], it would follow that the word expressing it is meaningless. And if the connection were established through what is implied, then in that case too, the connection would necessarily result in [the word] referring to the agent alone.
What indeed is the difference between the two verbs *hupyate* and *svapiti* with respect to the implication of an agent?
It might be argued: by the force of grammatical rules such as Pāṇini’s *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (A 1.3.13), the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*) are expressed by the suffixes;
consequently, the number denoted by those [suffixes] is construed with them.
But where a factor has not arisen therein, the number denoted by that [term] applies,
according to the principle: "Or rather, the primary [meaning] prevails because of the prior injunction, as in common worldly usage" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 12.2.23).
The rule that [the suffix] resorts only to the agent according to this logic is not tenable, because it would lead to the opposite conclusion. This is evident from the rules:
"After the remaining roots, the *parasmaipada* suffixes are used when the agent is expressed" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.78) and "The *śap* augment is used when the agent is expressed" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.68).
Thus, by the force of the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*), the agent and the object are expressed by the suffix;
consequently, the number denoted by that [suffix] is also construed with those two.

As for the suffix that has not arisen in that context, the number denoted by it would, according to the same principle, pertain only to the object; since such a restriction is logically consistent, one should therefore abandon the "mud of confusion" and follow the grammatical rule exactly as it is.
It follows, therefore, that it is apprehended.

To this objection, it is replied: "When the number to be expressed is already obtained through implication (ākṣepa), there is no need to postulate a further denotation (abhidhāna). Even when the mere object to be numbered is obtained, its determination occurs through expectancy (sākāṅkṣa). (Ku. 5.657)
This enumeration follows the meditative cultivation (bhāvanā);
for it is established that whatever the cultivation follows, that very thing is enumerated.
Because there is a rule that [a verbal root] must be expressed by a single suffix;
furthermore, the efficient force (bhāvanā) requires only the pure meaning of the nominal stem,
for an operation does not depend upon that which already possesses an operation.
Because it would reside in itself (258),
because it is of no utility with respect to inherence,
and because that which possesses an operation of a different genus cannot be an agent.

Furthermore, there are no case-endings other than the first [the nominative] for nominal stems. Therefore, since it is established that the *bhāvanā* connects only with that which is indicated by the nominative, and because of this restriction regarding its fitness for connection, number—which follows that [nominative]—also connects with that very same [subject]; thus, there is no over-extension, just as in the case of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*). For example, as in "Caitra is not a Brāhmaṇa" or "not [a Brāhmaṇa]."

In expressions such as "The fair-complexioned one does not throb" (*gauraḥ na spandate*) or "The one with earrings does not [throb]" (*na kuṇḍalī*), although there is a specific co-occurrence of qualifier and qualified, and although there is no difference in the fact that the negative particle (*nañ*) does not denote them, the meaning of the negative particle connects only with the portions that are qualifiers, and not with the portion that is the qualified. Now, it might be argued: "In those cases, it is so because of sublation (*bādhāt*)."
For if it were connected with the qualified object (viśeṣya), the mention of the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) would not be purposeful,

since the negation of the qualifier is already understood through the negation of that [qualified object] alone; moreover, if both were negated, there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda) due to repetition.
If it is argued that there is no recurrence [of the verb] because it is already complete (nirākāṅkṣa), we reply that this is equal [in both cases].

For when the syntactic connection (anvaya) projected by the efficient force (bhāvanā) conveyed by the same suffix is possible, it is more cumbersome to abandon what is proximate and adopt what is remote in the absence of a subverting reason. Furthermore, even if the efficient force projects a general [connection], if one abandons that which requires a complement (sākāṅkṣa), a connection with that which lacks such a requirement (nirākāṅkṣa) is impossible.
For it is not the expectancy of one alone that is the cause of syntactic connection (*anvaya*), but rather the expectancy of both.

Indeed, the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), failing to obtain connection with a result, requires a relation with an action; and the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), being itself an operation, requires an agent of that operation. Thus, the expectancy of both is the cause of syntactic connection.

However, in cases such as "the mat by means of the mat," the factor is already endowed with the result by virtue of being a *kāraka* itself; it does not require another operation and is thus free of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*).

For this very reason, in expressions such as "it is sat" (*āsyate*) or "it is slept" (*sūpyate*), there is no syntactic connection with an implied [agent]. Indeed, the word ending in the third case, "by Caitra" (*caitreṇa*), has no expectancy toward the productive operation (*bhāvanā*).

If it is argued that there is an expectancy for an object to be brought about (*bhāvya*), we say no; because [the root] is connected with the fruit, which is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) such as "lying down" (*śayana*).
Furthermore, in this context, that which is related to the fruit is not distinct from the agent (*kartṛ*).
For meanings of verbal roots such as "lying down" are never connected with anything other than the agent.
Furthermore, there is no other entity called "that which is to be produced" (*bhāvya*) apart from the fruit and its relation [to the agent], such that one would have to depend upon it.
It might be argued: why is it not the case that one says, for example, "The mat makes Caitra"?
If it is argued that this is because there would be no distinction between what is expressed and what is unexpressed, we say no; for the form *cetram* ending in the nominative case is ungrammatical.

However, since the form ending in the accusative case denotes the object (*karman*), the efficient force (*bhāvanā*)—being connected with that [object] and thus not requiring another thing to be brought into being (*bhāvya*)—would require only the agent (*bhāvaka*).
Nor does the mat possess the capacity to manifest Caitra, because they are distinct entities.
However, when there is a desire to speak, an unreliable person certainly employs such expressions.
But let it be employed—such as "Caitra makes a mat" and so forth—it cannot be, because such a statement fails to convey the meaning of the sentence due to its being eternally ambiguous.
If it is argued that, because the distinction [of the agent] is not manifested for the sake of its production, let it then be manifested by the third case as "by Caitra";
or, if it is argued that in the case of "Devadatta makes a mat," let it be manifested by the second case—[we reply: no, because such usage does not occur.
For even an untrustworthy person does not employ such expressions [as "gārgikayā"].
If it is asked, "How is it that this alone is so, provided there is no contradiction with the grammatical definition?"—it is because the world is not subject to questioning.
Indeed, the word *gārgikayā* is not employed independently, without regard for its proximity to a word expressing praise, such as *sādhu*.
If it is argued that this is because [the action] is enjoined by that very qualification (upādhi), then from what does this follow?
If it is argued that it is because such usage is observed in common worldly practice, then the same applies here:
[the word] "karoti" and so forth are employed only in conjunction with a case ending denoting an object (*karma-vibhakti*).
Since it is said "it is done" (*kriyate*), this must necessarily be expressed through the co-occurrence with the agentive case-ending (*kartṛvibhakti*); what else could be done here?

It is precisely by accepting this distinction that the grammatical rule governing the topic of "non-expression" (*anabhihitādhikāra*) finds a place in the hearts of all. Therefore, the division between expression and non-expression is indeed elegant when it comes to the stage of formal instruction.

It might be argued: "Let it be granted that *bhāvanā* is common to all verbal suffixes; yet, when connected with a specific time, it is the meaning of the *laṭ* and other suffixes, whereas when not touched by the three times, it is the meaning of the optative (*liṅ*) suffix. This is not so, because it would follow that it has the same meaning as the word "effort" (*yatna*).

If it is argued that there is a distinction based on whether there is coloring by the object (*viṣayoparāga*) or no coloring by the object, we say no—because this would result in its being synonymous with "the effort of sacrifice" (*yāgayatna*).

If it is argued that there is a distinction based on whether the number of the agent (*kartṛsaṅkhyā*) is expressed or not expressed, we say no—because this would result in its being identical to "one who possesses the effort of sacrifice" (*yāgayatnavān*).
If it is argued that this meaning is indeed intended, we say no—because even after a hundred years from now, [people] would still not engage in [such an interpretation].

If it is argued that [the person] does not act because there is no mention of a fruit [in the injunction], we say no; for even from the statement "one who desires heaven should possess the effort to perform sacrifice," there would still be no activity.
Why is that?
Because an effort is not [the cause] of an effort.
The cause is either the cognition of effort or the cause of effort; however, it is rather desire (*icchā*).
Nor is that [desire] itself produced by effort such that it alone should be understood as the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*); rather, [it is the cause] by its mere existence.
Nor does that [cognition] exist at the time the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is heard;
nor does the optative suffix itself produce it, for it cannot do so without conveying a specific meaning. (261)
Because if that [word] were the producer [of the cognition], the acquisition of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) would be useless;
furthermore, it would follow that no desire to act would arise from unperceived inferential marks (*liṅga*).
By this, it is also refuted that linguistic convention, arising from the usage of elders, must rely upon that very thing understood by the child to be the cause of activity within himself.
The view that this [activity] proceeds merely from the resolve "I shall do it myself," and therefore that resolve alone is the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), is refuted.
For what would this "I shall do" be: an effort (*prayatna*) or a desire (*icchā*)?
Not the first, because it is contradictory for something to operate upon itself;
nor the second,
for that [activity] produces effort by its very existence alone.
And it has been stated that at the time of hearing the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*), that [desire for the fruit] does not exist;
for even though the desire for the fruit is naturally flowing, it is not a cause for effort,
because its object is something else.
And for that reason, the treatise would be purposeless;
for since that [nature] is established through other causes alone, there would be no need for a treatise even to cognize it,
as it is already cognizable by the mind.
And the scripture is purposeful regarding what has not been attained;
for when something is already attained, there is no occasion for the scripture.
Furthermore, if that were stated, there would be a redundancy regarding the qualification of the agent by the phrase "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*).
For in that case, the meaning of the word "should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) itself would be "the performer of the sacrifice is one who desires heaven.
Moreover, if [an injunction] directed toward the fruit were to produce an effort directed toward the means, [it would be illogical].

One might act [toward something] elsewhere as well, since there is no restricting factor (*niyāmaka*). If it is argued that the causal relationship itself (*hetuphalabhāva*) is the restricting factor—[we reply: No; for if that [relationship] were a restricting factor when it is unknown, it would follow that one would engage in a sacrifice even without [hearing] a Vedic injunction (*liṅ*), merely from a desire for heaven. However, if its being a means to that [result] is the restricting factor when it is known, then that very desire [for the result] must impel one toward it; for there is a rule: "Whoever desires X necessarily desires the means to X."
Nor is it the case that she exists at that time,
nor is it logical to claim that the knowledge of her alone generates the effort, and that this [knowledge] is produced by the optative suffix (liṅ).
Furthermore, because it would follow that even one who merely desires heaven—that is, one who has a mere wish to perform a sacrifice—would be prompted to act;

or else, upon understanding the optative suffix (*liṅ*) as denoting desire, everyone, even those lacking such a desire, would be prompted to act. If it is argued that the cognition of it occurs as being connected to oneself and not in a general sense, we say no: for if it were not expressed by the third person, it would follow that the optative does not have the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*).
Furthermore, because activity would result even from the thought, "You desire rice," [and] "You wish to cook"; moreover, if effort were to arise from the cognition of a resolution (*saṅkalpa*),
then from what would that resolution itself be born, and for what purpose?
If it is argued that [the effort] arises from the very knowledge of the intention and for the sake of exertion— [we reply: surely, intention is a particular kind of desire,
and that [desire] is by its very nature directed toward pleasure.
And if that [desire] is adventitious (*aupādhika*) in its accomplishment,
how can it have volition as its object?
If you say, "Because it is the means to that [accomplishment]," then [it follows that desire cannot exist] due to the lack of knowledge regarding its being such a means.
But it cannot arise from the mere knowledge of the nature of volition;
otherwise, even the knowledge that something is a means to a desired end would become useless.
Therefore, it must be accepted that volition is the motivator.
However, because it exists merely as a presence and is not known, it is not an injunction;
and since knowledge brings about practical activity only by presenting an object, that which remains is necessarily the object itself.

Thus is the refutation of [the action] as a property of the agent. Let it then be a property of the object; no, it is said, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), nor is it the fruit, nor is it the *apūrva*, for that would entail the loss of its true nature.
Because that [result] is not obtained, there is neither an effect nor an action, due to the lack of commencement. For [the object of desire] must be either the fruit or its cause, the *apūrva*.
Is that [desire] the cause or the action?
Not the first, because the desire for the fruit is not the cause of the initiation of activity.
Because it has already been stated that this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*),
the second [alternative] is not tenable, as there is no established understanding (*avyutpatti*).
For the ground for the activity [induced] by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) must be either "novelty" (*apūrvatva*),
or "task-to-be-accomplished-ness" (*kāryatva*), or both.
It is not the first [alternative].

For if the "novelty" (*apūrvatva*) that serves as the ground for the application of the word were understood through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), its status as "novelty" would be contradicted; if it were not so understood, there would be no linguistic competency (*avyutpatti*);
and because, without the cognition of the relatum, it is impossible to comprehend the relation itself.
For that very reason, [the understanding of the meaning] would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

Nor is it reasonable to claim that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) applies to the *apūrva* by means of the motive of "being unprecedented" (*apūrvatva*), which is presented through "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) without great remoteness— just as the word "earth" (*pṛthivī*) applies to earth when it is presented as possessing fragrance.

In this case, since both [earthness and being an effect] are equally perceived, when a doubt arises, it is logical that the application of the inferential mark (saṅgati) comes to rest upon earthness alone by virtue of the principle of parsimony (kalpanā-gaurava);
however, there is no perception of "novelty" (apūrvatva) here.
It might be argued: "This inferential mark (liṅga) proceeded by taking 'being an effect' as its secondary indicator (upalakṣaṇa)."

And neither the sacrifice characterized by that [desire], nor the effort, nor anything else within the scope of non-verbal means of knowledge, is capable of being a means to heaven as a qualification for the person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikārin*).
Nor can one who desires a fruit be enjoined toward that which has no desired fruit. Therefore, something else entirely non-worldly (*alaukika*) is indicated by this [desire].
If it is asked, "What is unestablished about [the claim] that [the meaning of a word] is the object of the operation of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth?"—we reply: No;
for remembrance or inference would be the indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Yet both of these are impossible without a previously apprehended relation (*sambandha*).

For being an effect does not characterize "novelty" (*apūrvatva*) in the same way that being a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskāra*), being the mind (*manas*), or being the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) does,
because it depends upon cognition;
just as an elephant [indicates] its keeper.
Just as one might infer fire from smoke through the knowledge of their relationship, so too should one discern it,
and not otherwise.
And thus, even the attempt to establish this through logic is like crying out in the wilderness;
for even with a thousand arguments, one cannot grasp the linguistic connection (*saṅgati*) regarding what is unknown, nor does a word function when its connection remains ungrasped.
By this, the view that the acquisition of linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) regarding the effect of an action arises from the non-apprehension of difference is refuted.
For the non-apprehension of difference regarding what is unknown cannot be a factor in linguistic usage, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, if a previously unknown [property] were postulated as the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), it would follow that the worldly optative suffix (*liṅ*) would be rendered meaningless.
In that case, because there is no object to be characterized [by a secondary sense],

if it is argued that "being an effect" alone is the basis for the application [of the term] there, then let it be exactly so in the present case as well, since it is already established and is possible.

[Ku. 5.665] Suppose, then, that this alone is the basis for linguistic usage (*pravṛttinimitta*), and that the acquisition of a previously unestablished individual instance occurs through the application of reasoning (*tarka*). If this is argued, we say no—because it would follow that there could be no acquisition of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) in the case of eternal injunctions or prohibitions. Furthermore, under this view, one cannot apply a scriptural meaning determined in one instance to another.
In that very way, linguistic usage is possible,
because it has been determined that "being an effect" (kāryatva) alone is the basis for engagement (pravṛttinimitta),
and not "novelty" (apūrvatva).
Furthermore, because it is impossible for that [general form] to be brought about through logical necessity (*nyāya*),
for a specific individual is obtained in accordance with the fruit;
and that [specific individual] is not heard of there [in the Vedic injunction].
Nor can that which is not even heard be postulated,
because there is no seed for it;
for it could only be postulated through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the injunction.
Or [it might be argued] that it is by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the cognition of something as an effect, as in the world.
Not the first [alternative],
because in your own system, that [cognition] is of the nature of what is to be attained (*upeya*).
For, even though heaven is known from scripture to be the fruit, an increase in the goal is still asserted.
It is not the second [alternative]; for if that [increase] were cognized through the force of the words themselves, there would be no dependence upon it.
For it is accepted that in the world, the cognition of something as a means to a desired end depends upon that [prior experience], whereas in the Veda it does not;
otherwise, the fact of being a means to a desired end would have to be understood first from the Veda itself.
Because there is no other means of valid cognition [for it],
the injunction would therefore be inferential based on its being an effect, not verbal.
Let the result be inferential.
Nor is it correct to argue that there is a pervasion (vyāpti) such that "whatever is to be done is a means to a desired end," because this is contradicted by the case of pleasure (*sukha*).
If you say that the qualification "provided it is something other [than the end itself]" applies, no— because this is still contradicted by the absence of suffering (*duḥkhābhāva*).
If it is argued that [the result] is abandoned, then what exactly has been said?
If it is argued that it is desired by its own nature, then that which is other than it would be undesired; and since that [undesired thing] must be produced, there is a contradiction.

If it is argued that this [is] its means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), then the qualification "while being its means of accomplishment" is indistinguishable from the probandum (*sādhya*). If it is argued that the meaning of the proof is: "This is not desired by its own nature, yet it is to be performed;
therefore, it must surely be a means for accomplishing what is desired," we say no, because the premise "this is not desired by its own nature" is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Because it is pervaded by an activity that proceeds without aiming at anything else;
otherwise, that [activity] would not be established. Therefore, due to this contradiction, one of the two must be abandoned.

If it is argued, "Let there be no attainment of the eternal (nitya) and the unprecedented (apūrva); what is lost to us?"— what is lost to us when that non-attainment occurs even in the context of rites performed for specific desires (kāmya-adhikāra)?

For it is not the case that the *liṅ* suffix expresses the action as a means to heaven; nor is it obtained through the otherwise inexplicable co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), since [that co-occurrence] is sufficiently explained merely by its delimiting the qualified agent (*adhikārin*), just as in the case of [the mention of] being a Brāhmaṇa and so forth.
Nor is this an inference— namely, that "whatever is to be done by someone due to his own desire is a means to achieve what is desired by him"—
because it is not established that something is to be done by its own nature (rather than through desire).
For, by that very [desire], the necessity of performing that [action] is easily shown to be non-conclusive;
and because an adventitious necessity cannot be understood without understanding its status as a means to a desired end,
what is the use of this consideration of distinctions?
If it is argued that an inference is established merely by the fact that it is perceived from a word that one effect is intended when another is produced— [we reply: surely,
what is to be denoted must be that which is already connected [to the meaning].
And that which is appropriate is what is connected; for one who desires one thing, another must be performed, which is unfit for connection—
how then could that be expressed?
If it is argued that the status of being a means to that [desired end] is established from that very [word],

then, in that case, since the word expresses "what is to be done" (kartavyatva) as inhering in the same object as the status of being a means to the desired end, there is no room for inference. Nor is this the case in the theory of the expression of the related (anvitābhidhāna).
Nor is there the establishment of its being a means to that [result], for the capacity for syntactic connection is established even by the mere delimitation of the qualified person (*adhikārī*).
Furthermore, the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is not possible in the case of the *apūrva*.
For if it were the state of being pervaded by an effort (*kṛti*), it would apply only to rice and the like,
because they are already established [as accomplished].
If it were the state of being the fruit of an effort, it would apply only to the sacrifice.
Because it arises immediately thereafter,
if there is an objectivity based on purpose, it belongs to heaven alone,
since it is naturally beautiful.
But it does not belong to the apūrva, because that is the opposite of this.
If it is argued that [the agency] is adventitious (aupādhikī), like the drinking of breast milk and so forth, we reply: even that belongs to the sacrifice itself.

Since heaven is established as the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it is joined [in the injunction] precisely as the sacrifice is the means (*sādhana*). If it is argued that this does not work because of the temporal separation [between the act and its result], we reply: let it be so postulated in accordance with the revealed scripture (*śruti*) as it does indeed work. (267)
“It might somehow be [possible] by way of an operation;

however, there can be no relationship of ‘possessor of operation’ and ‘operation’ between two things existing at different times. And it is through an operation that the status of being a cause is logically connected.”
If it is argued that reality consists in being immediately prior in time,
because otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), we say no; for causality consists merely in the necessity of prior existence,
and an intermediate effect that conforms to the final effect is itself what constitutes the operation (*vyāpāra*).
[Objection: It is because such usage is common in agriculture, medicine, and so forth.
[Response: If you say this is merely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), it is not so; for there is no contradiction in its being used in its primary sense (*mukhyārtha*).
Let it be, then, that when a Brahmin is killed by his son, the long-deceased father is the agent by making that intermediate operation (the son's act) his own.

If it is argued that, in such a case, the course of worldly affairs would collapse—[we reply: no, because even when a son exists, [the father] sometimes does not perform [the funeral rites], and because even when he does not exist, [the rites] are sometimes performed; thus, since it cannot be the means of accomplishment (*anirvāhakatā*), it cannot be considered an operation (*vyāpāra*).
For only that which, having been produced, ensures the prior existence of another with respect to a specific effect, is the operation of that [cause] with respect to that [effect], and nothing else.
As, for example, the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is the operation of experience with respect to recollection.

For in that case, since the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) is established, the latent impression (saṃskāra) is postulated by the principle of "otherwise it would be inexplicable" (anyathānupapatti), and not otherwise; so it is here as well.
If this were not so, then according to your own view as well, there could be no agency for one who is struck down at the very same moment as the arrow capable of piercing Brahmā is released.
And it might belong to his father as he lies in his own dwelling;
by this, the view that "neither [of these two] exists" is refuted.
[Ku. 5.668] Let it be, then, that "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is simply the property of action (*kriyādharma*), and this is the injunction (*vidhi*).

For everyone understands, "This must be done," and then, having formed the intention (*saṅkalpa*) "I shall do it," one engages in activity—if you argue thus, we say no; for the meaning of the verbal suffix *kṛtya* would have to be the determination (*adhyavasāya*) that "this must be done by me."
Or could it mean "that which is appropriate for me to do"?
In that case, the first [option] does not differ from a mere mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*);
for the thought "I must do this" is indeed a resolve regarding an action that is yet to be performed.
However, the intention regarding a proximate action is "I shall do," and that is not the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*);
for it has been stated that [the optative] incites by its mere existence.
This [injunction] impels one once the sense of "this must be done" has arisen; however, in the actual state of things, this is understood by the deluded as occurring when that sense is already known.
Propriety (*aucitya*), moreover, is a property of the action consisting in its prior non-existence, or, when that exists, its feasibility.
If that [non-existence] exists,
does it serve as a benefit to the agent? In the first case, it would not cease from anything whatsoever.
In the second case, one would likewise engage even with such suffering;
however, regarding the third case, it will be said later:
"Let it then be an instrumental property"—no, for sound is not an instrument.
That property may be the denotation itself,
or its object such as *bhāvanā* and so forth, or it may be the quality of being a means to achieve the desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*).

Not the first [alternative], because of non-existence and because of the lack of activity; nor is even the designation more significant, since the subverting argument is equal [in force]. Thus, even the remaining alternative is difficult to establish. //13//
Because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that [connection] which would exceed the mere conjunction and re-union;
for even that which inheres in one thing may be established as the operation of another, like a *pūrva* (unseen force);
and this is also the case with respect to its being an object (*viṣayatā*).

And because its own operation, like that of a logical mark (liṅga), does not contradict its status as a cause; for even when there is an excess [of conditions], activity does not arise from it, whereas among the ignorant, such activity occurs even in the absence of that [excess].
For even those who hear it through another word do not engage [in action];
nor is that object of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) something entirely distinct,
since its distinction from that [other word] is a matter of cognition (*pratipatti*).
If it is with respect to [a specific] activity, then there must also be a specific object; if it is with respect to mere activity in general,
how can it be said that the word is inherent in the denotation?
If it is argued that [the self exists] because of its proximity [to the body], we say no; for there is no fixed rule [for such proximity].
If it is argued that this is not so because everything else has been negated, we say no; for the negation of [anything else] being the cause of activity is equal [in the case of the self as well].
Furthermore, it is impossible to negate the proximity of that [self].
Furthermore, if it were cognizable solely through verbal testimony, there would be no linguistic acquisition (*avyutpatti*).

As for the claim that "linguistic acquisition is established through the otherwise inexplicability of purposeful activity" (*pravṛttyanyathānupapatti*), that too is worthless; for one does not engage in activity simply because there exists some cause for activity.
Rather, it must be the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*).

For it is established by universal experience that everyone connects [the action] with the thought, "This being performed by me will accomplish my desired goal"; from that, one desires, "May I do it"; and from that, one acts.
Therefore, this person seeking to learn, having obtained a desire that generates effort from a certain cognition,
infers that very cognition to be the cause of the listener's inclination upon hearing the optative suffix (*liṅ*).

Consequently, he determines that the meaning of the optative suffix is "being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatā*), which inheres in the same object as "that which is to be done" (*kartavyatā*).
Nor should it be argued: "If that is the case, let there simply be 'what ought to be done' (kartavyatā), since that must necessarily be accepted;
what is the use of [positing] 'being a means to a desired end' (iṣṭasādhanatā)?"—for one does not act merely upon perceiving that something is a means to a desired end.

Because there is deviation in the case of what is impossible to accomplish— thus, experience shows that an agent proceeds to action after understanding that the object of effort possesses the quality of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*).
In that context, the "object" (*viṣaya*) is expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*), while the "productive operation" (*bhāvanā*) is expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) alone.

As for the remainder, by the force of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), once the status of being a means to a desired end has been understood through the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in its specific sense, there arises the comprehension that the object of that suffix is a means to achieve what is desired. Thus, it has been stated that the "status of being a means to a desired end," which inheres in the same substrate as the "obligatory nature" (*kartavyatā*), is the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the optative suffix.

As for the objection that the instrumental case ending in *jyotiṣṭomena* would be improper if the optative were expressing the instrument’s status as a means to the desired end—that criticism is to be utterly disregarded by anyone who is not a grammarian.
For the denotation of that [number] is indeed the denotation of it by means of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*);
and that is not present in the current context. Nor does the optative suffix (*liṅ*) denote that the sacrifice is a means to a desired end.
However, it has been stated that its attainment occurs through the force of positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
As for the fact that the status of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) is also understood from the instruction of an authoritative person (*siddhopadeśa*);

Nor should it be objected that there is no activity whose nature is mere conceptualization (*saṅkalpa*); for who could deny that even when one possesses the capacity and a powerful desire for a result, there may still be no activity toward the means to achieve it? Furthermore, since this point and its refutation are common to all positions, what is the point of raising it?
To this it is replied: Let it be granted that the status of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*), which inheres in the object of effort, is the cause of inclination (*pravṛtti*);
nevertheless, this is not the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), because of doubt.
For is that [status] understood directly from the optative suffix itself, or...

A doubt arises as to whether [the child] acts like an infant who, through inference and so forth, engages in suckling at the breast, or whether [the word] is inferred from some object established by that [word], just as a person conversant with convention infers a specific intention from a specific gesture.

And this being the case, the conclusion is simply that it is not denoted: "Because of its being a cause, because of inference, because of its absence in the middle and at the beginning, because of its capacity being established elsewhere, and because negation would otherwise be untenable. (14)
For instance, having heard the injunction, "One who desires fire should rub two pieces of wood together," when asked "Why?", speakers reply,
"Because from that rubbing, fire is accomplished for him.
(He crosses over death?)

In such passages as "He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice overcomes the murder of a Brahmin," once the status of the act as a desired means has been understood, the experts in the system (tāntrikas) infer the injunction:
"One desiring to overcome death and the murder of a Brahmin should perform the Aśvamedha sacrifice," and they infer the prohibition from the corresponding censure.
For example, from the passage, "Those people who destroy themselves enter blind darkness," it follows that one should not destroy oneself.

In cases such as "you should do" or "I shall do," the optative suffix (*liṅ*) prescribed by the rule of injunction does not express the state of being a means to a desired end; rather, it expresses the intention of the speaker.

The meaning of the word "I shall do" is not that "this is my desired means," but rather it is the volition (*saṅkalpa*) "I shall do" that arises immediately following the cognition of that [means]. Furthermore, it is established that in all other cases as well, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) expresses the desire of the speaker alone.

For thus, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) shines forth with [the meanings of] command (*ājñā*), entreaty (*adhyeṣaṇā*), permission (*anujñā*), inquiry (*sampraśna*), request (*prārthanā*), and benediction (*āśaṃsā*).
Among these, that which does not conform to the speaker’s desire and fears agitation from it is "command.
That, however, which manifests respect and honor for the listener—
That [request] is an entreaty;
permission is that which indicates the absence of prohibition;
and inquiry is that which has the purpose of eliciting an expression.
Greed is desire; prayer is the wishing for what is auspicious; and benediction is the expression of such a wish. Furthermore, a prohibition is not logically applicable to injunctions or alternatives.
For instance, when the expression is a positive injunction (*vidhi*),
then the sentence-meaning— that "one should not kill," meaning the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of killing is not enjoined— is refuted by contradiction.
When the cultivation [of the object] is not touched by the three times, then, in relation to the word "not," the absolute non-existence is false;
when it is an effect, [it is real].
In that case,
the claim that "one should not kill"— meaning killing should not be performed— is contrary to experience,
because it is indeed performed.

Nor is there the view that "there is no purpose in killing" in the sense that "there is no effect caused by killing," because either the cessation of suffering or the attainment of happiness exists therein.

The meaning is that there is no unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*, *apūrva*) caused by killing; thus, the scriptural sense is sound, as it would certainly impel one who seeks a visible result to act without fear.
However, the idea that one should produce an unseen merit through non-killing is impossible, because since the cause is beginningless, it would follow that the effect must likewise be so.
And because that [non-killing] is not an object of cultivation (*bhāvanā*);
by the resolve (*saṅkalpa*) "I shall not kill," there would either have to be an uninterrupted resolve toward it for as long as one lives,
or else cessation would occur immediately upon performing it once.
One may indeed kill afterwards, as there is no contradiction;
for the purpose of the injunction has been accomplished by him.
The meaning of the sentence is: "To the extent that one possesses the intention to kill, to that same extent one should cultivate the contrary intention to produce the *apūrva*."
The claim that "one who has become such [a knower] possesses the qualification" is also untenable, because that is not heard [in the scriptures].
If it is argued that "only what is possible is prohibited, not what is impossible," we reply: nothing at all is prohibited here.
The meaning of the negation is that its absence is being established; the sentence-meaning is the *apūrva* (transcendental result) produced by the act of forming the resolve not to kill.
Furthermore, from the Veda there arises the cognition that "one should not kill" implies an unseen merit (*apūrva*) as something to be performed;
yet, once this has arisen, one proceeds toward the act of killing out of passion.

To say, "One should certainly kill," on the grounds of the maxim that "an expected fruit is weightier than a fruitless duty"—oh, what skill in explaining the Veda shown by this stubborn Mīmāṃsaka who prides himself on his orthodoxy! (272)
Even on the view that [the meaning of the prohibition] is the state of being a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatā*),
the sentence-meaning would be "one should not kill"— that is, "the mental disposition toward killing (*hananabhāvanā*) is not a means to what is desired.
In that case, how could the fact that it is a means to what is undesired (*aniṣṭasādhanatva*) be obtained?
For it is not observed that whatever is not a means to achieve what is desired is necessarily a means to achieve what is undesired,
because there also exists that which is to be disregarded (*upekṣaṇīya*).
"That which is prohibited for one who is attached to passion and so forth is necessarily observed to be a means to achieve what is undesired."
The argument that "just as one would not eat food mixed with poison,
so too [the Veda] will be inferred in the case of the Veda" is also not sound, because it is precisely the meaning of the prohibition that is being considered;

for it is impossible to establish the non-existence of the state of being something to be done (*kartavyatva*), the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), or the productive activity (*bhāvanā*).

If it is argued that this is because worldly things are established by worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), we reply: even so, it cannot be established [in that way]—because there is no certainty [of truth] due to the refutation of the scriptures of heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*). If it is argued that those [heretical scriptures] are not valid means of knowledge, we reply: no, because since they do not differ in their presentation of objects contrary to reality, these [worldly things] would likewise be of such a nature.

If it is argued that validity [of the Upaniṣads] exists by way of their purport (*tātparya*), we say no—because injunctions and prohibitions do not have anything else as their primary purpose, according to the statement: "In an injunction, the literal meaning of the word is not secondary.

If it is further argued that this might nevertheless be the case for a prohibition, we say no—because there is an absence of both an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) and an activity directed toward that [prohibition].

Nor does this negative particle (*nañ*) have the sense of denoting a contradiction, as in the case of "non-asura" (*an-asura*) or "ignorance" (*avidyā*); for it is connected with a verb and is not part of a compound.

Therefore—[Kumārila 5.678]: "Injunction (*vidhi*) is the speaker’s intention, which is denoted by the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth in relation to activity and the like; however, the status of being a desired means for the agent is what is to be inferred. (15)

In that regard, there is the expression of the desire for an action whose agent is oneself, as in "I shall do"; the expression of the desire for an action whose agent is the person being addressed, as in "one should do";
and the expression of the desire for an action whose agent is another, as in "one should cause [another] to do."
Thus, the meaning of the worldly statement "one desiring fire should rub two pieces of wood" results in this:
"My desired goal is the activity of one desiring fire toward the rubbing of wood.
From that, the listener infers:
Surely the effort to churn wood is a means for fire;
for whatever object an effort is intended by an authoritative person, that [object] is the required cause for that [effort].
And it has been understood by him in such a way that [the object] is the domain of eating for my own son and others, because of the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
The meaning of "one should not eat poison" is that my inclination toward the act of eating poison is not desired by me. From this, the listener likewise infers:
"Surely, the mental disposition toward eating poison is a means to what is undesirable."

For whatever object an effort is directed toward— even if it accomplishes what the agent desires— if it is not accepted by a reliable person (āpta), that object is a cause of even greater misfortune for him,
and he has understood it as such.
This is because of the pervasion (vyāpti) that this mode of action— such as playing with one's own children or consuming mud and poison—
is observed only in worldly speech; it is only in such worldly sentences that this manner of expression ever enters the intellect.
If it is argued that [the person] does not exist in the Vedic [context], because the person has been rejected therein, we say no—because there is no reason for such a rejection.
If it is argued that even if such a reason existed, there is no proof for its existence, we reply: let there be no other [proof].
In the case of a maiden, scripture alone is the authority regarding her union with a man, just as the ritual injunction is the authority for a pregnancy;
what can be done here? Or rather, [what can be done] when the indicative power (*liṅ*) transcends its worldly meaning?
"Those very [sounds] which are worldly are the same as those which are Vedic, and their meanings are the same"—this view would collapse.
And thus, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that they are meaningless, like the sounds "ja-ba-ḍa-da-śa" and so forth; therefore, remain at ease [in your position].
It might be argued as follows:

Even so, if it is argued that the intention of the speakers—the teachers themselves—must reside in the injunction (*vidhi*) within the Veda, and that there is no need for an independent speaker such as the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), we reply: No; for they act merely with the intention of repetition (*abhyāsa*) because they are reciters (*anuvaktṛ*), like a parrot, and thus lack such an [independent] intention. Or, even if such an intention were present, the intention of one who merely repeats a royal edict is not itself a command (*ājñā*).
"What indeed belongs to the king alone?"—such is worldly experience.
Furthermore, from scripture: "For this entire Veda has the Supreme Lord as its object;
its purport, however, lies in the injunction [of ritual], by means of its own literal sense, just as [the purport of texts concerning] heaven and so forth lies in the injunction. (16)
Indeed, there are no portions of the Vedas where the Supreme Lord is not celebrated;
for instance, he is praised as the Creator in the Puruṣa Sūktas.
He exists as sovereign power among the Rudras,
as the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman) among the Maṇḍala-Brāhmaṇas, and, placing transcendence before all else, as the state beyond conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañcatā) in the Upaniṣads.

He is present as the Sacrificial Person (*yajñapuruṣa*) in the ritual injunctions of the mantras, through the manifestations of his body in the narrative accounts, and as the object of worship everywhere.
If it is argued that they are not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because their objects have already been established, we say no;
for the removal of suspicion regarding defects in the cause (*kāraṇadoṣaśaṅkānirāsa*) is common to both [types of objects], namely those yet to be realized and those that are already existent.
If it is argued that these [scriptures] have their purport elsewhere, [we reply] that this is by way of establishing their own literal meaning.
Or is it by virtue of being mere sound? In the first case, validity must be admitted even with respect to its own meaning,
because that meaning is not established by any other means of valid cognition.
Therefore, the claim that it serves as a mere reminder in that context is also false.

If you argue that even though it conveys that meaning, the primary purport (*tātparya*) does not lie there—then what fault is there in its having a purport elsewhere as well, provided it does not abandon its own literal meaning? In that case, it would be like the science of astrology.
Otherwise, much would fall into disorder if the means of knowledge that establish the nature of heaven, hell, the *vrātya*, the *śrotriya*, and so forth were to lack authority.
If it is argued that [the latter] is so because they are not sublated (*abādhanāt*), then the same applies here;
for such [a person] does not exist.
If it is argued that [the Self] is seen somewhere [in the world], then heaven and so forth are also like that.

If it is argued that if those [heaven and so forth] were false, there would be the consequence of the futility of injunctions because those who desire them would not engage in [the prescribed acts], then here too there is the consequence of the futility of the injunctions for meditating upon Him. For if those [heaven and so forth] were false, then since the fruits such as *sālokya* (residing in the same world) and *sāyujya* (union) would also be false, what discerning person would meditate upon Him? Thus, the two cases are equal.
[Ku. 5.682] Also from the sentence (*vākya*).
For here, "sentence-hood" is intended to mean the capacity to convey a specific relation (*saṃsarga*) or distinction (*viśeṣa*).

And thus, the formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: whatever collection of words conveys a specific relation between things is preceded by a knowledge of that relation independent of those words, just like worldly [utterances]; and so too is the Vedic [collection of words].
And a refutation against the opposing view has been stated [at verse 5.683].
Furthermore, even from the perspective of specific numbers: "I was," "I shall be," and so forth—such numbers reside in the speaker.
Moreover, the designation of the branches [of the Veda] could not exist without an original proclamation. (17)
For previously, number was mentioned as something to be produced (*kārya*); now, however, it is stated as something to be conveyed (*pratipādya*).
To explain: it is well-established that the number expressed by the first person (*uttamapuruṣa*) follows the speaker.
Moreover, that application [of the word] is found almost everywhere in the Veda;
therefore, even by means of that [word] as expressed therein, that very same [object] must be understood,
otherwise there would be the consequence of a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*).
Alternatively, "specific designation" (*samākhyāviśeṣa*) refers to a specific number;
for specific designations such as "the Kāṭhaka" and "the Kālāpaka" are traditionally remembered as belonging to specific branches (*śākhā*).
And these [designations] do not depend merely upon the act of recitation.
This is because speakers are infinite in number;
nor do they have as their cause an excellence of speech,
for even in the case of teachers, there is rather the fault of making things otherwise despite their excellence.
Furthermore, because there is no excellence in merely imitating that recitation,
what would be the restrictive factor for determining how many speakers have been preeminent throughout beginningless saṃsāra?
Nor is it reasonable to claim that the name belongs to the first speaker.
Because you do not accept that;
or, if you do accept it, then he alone is our author of the Veda, so your disagreement is in vain.
It might be argued as follows:

"Being Brāhmaṇas, Kaṭhas and others are merely sub-divisions of caste; therefore, it is not unreasonable that a Vedic branch (śākhā) to be studied by them and whose contents are to be performed by them should be designated by their specific name. This is not so, because Kṣatriyas and others also have the right to study that very same branch.
Furthermore, that specific quality which belongs to a Brāhmaṇa does not exist in a Kṣatriya or others;
nor is there any Veda other than that of the Kṣatriyas and so forth.
Furthermore, there is no rule that those belonging to the Kaṭha school study only the Kaṭhaka and practice only its meaning,
for the migration between different recensions is generally observed.
If it is argued that this rule previously existed but now it has fallen into disorder— then, in that case, there is always only disorder.
Because there is no confusion regarding intermediate sub-classifications such as "Kaṭha" and so forth, this is simply a matter of the [Vedic] text's own course;
therefore, it must be established that this specific connection with a particular name is caused solely by the words of the original expounder.
Prosperity.

[Ku. 5.685] Thus, that Blessed One, having been heard of and inferred by some, is also perceived directly, because he possesses the property of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*), like a jar.
But how can he be seen if he is devoid of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for such perception?
For that complex—whether consisting of the external sense organs or the internal mind—is not possible in his case.
Because the eye and other [senses] have restricted objects, and because the mind lacks independence regarding external objects;

as it has been said: "In the absence of a cause, there is an absence of an effect," and so forth—[this does not follow], because it is impossible to negate a causal totality (*sāmagrī*) that is manifested solely by its effect.
Furthermore, it is observed that even when the external senses have ceased their activity, there occurs a direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of objects situated in distant places and times.
This is not merely memory, for it is more vivid than memory, since there is no subsequent reflection in dreams such as "I remember" or "it was remembered"; rather, one says, "I see."
It is because of the reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) that it is "seen.
Nor is the status of being an experience (*anubhavatva*) merely superimposed there, because it is not sublated;
furthermore, even things such as the cutting off of one's own head appear [in dreams] despite not having been previously experienced.
If you argue that this is a misconception regarding memory— if the meaning is that there is a misconception concerning the object of memory— then we agree.
But if you mean that there is a misconception within memory itself regarding its status as an experience;
That has already been refuted previously;
nor is it even possible,
for what has been determined by one form cannot be determined by another as that which delimits the cognition.
And thus, when a memory such as "that jar" has arisen, for one who is deluded, there would be the thought "I am experiencing that jar," but not "this jar";
for "this jar" is certainly not the form of the memory.
Therefore, this must be accepted as experience alone.

Furthermore, there is truth in some dream-experiences as well, due to their correspondence with reality. And that [truth], even if it occurs by chance like the "crow and the palm fruit," is not without a cause.
Otherwise, it would follow that all dream-cognitions would likewise possess such reality.
And here, the cause is indeed *dharma*;
and just like that born of karma, this [dharma] born of yoga is to be understood through the practice of yoga.
Because action (karman) and yoga possess equal security and efficacy, the experience of yogis is valid cognition (*pramā*) due to its being born of dharma,
and it is the fruit of perception (*pratyakṣa*) due to its being direct intuition (*sākṣātkāritva*).
However, the distinction is that what arises merely from the cultivation of phenomena not supported by [valid means of knowledge] is not *pramā* (valid cognition).
Therefore, the absence of its causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is unestablished.

If it is asked, "Even so, what is the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary case?"—[the answer is: it would follow that the injunctions for yoga, such as "Two Brahmans are to be known," and so forth, would be rendered useless.
Because it would be teaching a means that is impossible to carry out,
and because this is not an injunction for a knowledge that is not directly perceived;
for its purpose is already fulfilled by the injunction for Vedic study itself, which is limited to the knowledge of the meaning.
By this, atoms and the like are explained. With reference to such a [Self], it is heard in scripture: "There is no loss of the seer's vision," and "One only, without a second."
“He sees without eyes; he hears without ears”; “Two Brahmans are to be known: the higher and the lower”; “With sacrifice they sacrificed to the sacrifice.”
"The gods," [and] "The sacrifice is indeed the gods," and "The sacrifice is indeed Viṣṇu," and so forth.
And it is also recorded:
(Gītā) "Renouncing all duties, take refuge in Me alone," and "Perform action for My sake, O son of Kuntī, free from attachment."
"This world is bound by action other than that performed for the sake of sacrifice," and "The action performed for the sake of sacrifice dissolves in its entirety," and so forth;
furthermore, devotion to the Lord (īśvarapraṇidhāna) is taught in the *Sāṅkhyapravacana*.
This [merit] is acquired through sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma,
through "pūrtam" (works of public utility) such as the building of palaces,
and through "tapas" (asceticism) such as enduring cold and heat.

Even the great seers seek to know [Brahman] through the restraints (*yama*) such as non-violence, the observances (*niyama*) such as purity and contentment, and through yoga consisting of posture (*āsana*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and so forth.

Having understood that "when this is known, all this becomes known," and having heard it, one should become single-mindedly devoted to that [Reality]. As it is sung here: "Fix your mind on Me, be My devotee, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me; thus, with your self disciplined and making Me your supreme goal, you shall come to Me alone."
“Having known Me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the Great Lord of all worlds, and the friend of all beings, one attains peace. Thus,
when [the mind] has been repeatedly washed by the abundant waters of the confluence of the Vedas and logic, [it becomes pure].
Those whose hearts you do not occupy are those whose intentions consist of the essence of virtuous conduct. (277)

However, O Compassionate One, even those men who act contrary to what has been taught, yet who intensely contemplate your majesty, should be regarded by you with compassion at the proper time. (278) 18.
O you who are beautiful by nature, O true treasury of bliss, our hearts have long been immersed in you;
nevertheless, even now, they remain restless and are not yet satiated. (279)

Therefore, O Lord, quickly extend your compassion, so that when our minds have attained one-pointed concentration upon you, we may not undergo the torments of Yama again for hundreds of lifetimes. (19)
Thus, may this brilliant *Nītikusumāñjali*, which perfumes both the right and the left [hands], be offered;
whether it succeeds or not, may the Teacher of the Lord of the Immortals be pleased by this gift presented at his footstool. //20//
Thus ends the treatise *Nyāyakusumāñjali*, composed by the illustrious Udayana, who was marked with the title of *Nyāyācārya*.
Oṃ tat sat.
May this be an offering to Brahman.
May there be auspiciousness.
May there be prosperity.
I.
